The Yājñavalkya Smṛti:
Exposition of the Tenfold Causes [Auspicious Invocation]
[1.1] Salutation to the illustrious Great Preceptor Vikhanas.
[1.2] Salutation to the glorious Śrīnivāsa, the Supreme Brahman.

[1.3–4] In the *Śrīvaikhānasagṛhyasūtratātparyacintāmaṇi* composed by Śrī Śrīnivāsa Makhin, the exposition of the tenfold causes. [1.5–6] I pay homage to Vedāntadeśika, the son of Śrīnivāsārya, who was born in the Vaikhānasa lineage and is devoted to the worship of Veṅkaṭeśa.
I salute Śrī Veṅkaṭeśa, the Lord of all, the infinite, the primordial, the ocean of compassion, who is well-worshipped by all the gods;
I salute the venerable gurus, hundreds of them such as Bhṛgu, Kaśyapa, and others, who are the cause of the preservation and creation of the entire world.
I pay homage to the ocean of the Vaikhānasa tradition, which is filled with the rivers of Śruti and Smṛti, agitated by the waves of the scriptures, and possesses the pure water of devotion to Viṣṇu.
[1.11] By which the eye of those for whom other [systems of] Sūtras were devised has been cleared of darkness;
[1.12] for this Vaikhānasa Sūtra indeed bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
I bow to the supreme Sūtra-Upaniṣad, which proclaims its own majesty through the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and other sources, and which is devoted to the Supreme Self.
[The lineage, name, etc., of the commentator: [1.15] By the son of Govindācārya, born of the illustrious Kauśika lineage,
[1.16] whose soul is devoted to the service of the lotus feet of Śrī Veṅkaṭeśa;
[1.17] Following the path established by the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and so forth;
[1.18] adhering to the tradition well-trodden by the ancient teachers.
[1.19] By Śrīnivāsārya Yajvan, the most eminent among the teachers of Vedānta, [1.20] a commentary on the Vaikhānasa Sūtra is here clearly elucidated.

[The Exposition of the Tenfold Reasons for the Supremacy of the Vaikhānasa Sūtra and its Followers] [2.1–3] Now, regarding the supremacy of the Vaikhānasa Sūtra— composed by the four-faced Brahmā, who is denoted by the term *Vikhanaś* and born from the glorious Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman, who is distinguished by all auspicious qualities such as truthfulness and so forth— the following ten reasons are set forth.
Furthermore, ten reasons are set forth for the fact that those who practice the dharmas taught in that sūtra are the most preeminent of all.
[2.4] As follows:
[2.5–9] Because it was composed by Vikhanas, the cause of the entire world; because it is the first of all sūtras; and because, in all ritual acts...
Because it follows the path of the Vedas; because it sets forth all ritual actions accompanied by mantras; because it includes the sacraments such as *niṣeka*;
because it teaches the eighteen bodily sacraments (*saṃskāras*); because it possesses a complete collection of ancillary rites; because it has been accepted by Manu and others;
because its sole ultimate aim is the glorious Nārāyaṇa, the singular cause of the entire world; and [because it is for] those who perform the duties prescribed in these sūtras.
And because it is thus established that this is most dear to the Blessed One.

(2.10–12) By these reasons, the supremacy of this Sūtra among all Sūtras is demonstrated through the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and so forth, both because of its status as the best of all Sūtras and because the Vaikhānasas are the very best of all due solely to their practice of the dharmas taught in this Sūtra.

First, the reason is established: because it was composed by Vikhanas, who is the cause of the entire universe. [2.13] Determination of the meaning of the word *Vikhanas* [the fact that Nārāyaṇa is denoted by the words *Vikhanas*, *Vaikhānasa*, and so forth].
[2.14] Is there some sage named Vikhanas, or is it Nārāyaṇa?
It is Nārāyaṇa alone.

[2.15–16] Because there is no teaching that a mere sage (*muni*) is denoted by the term *vaikhānasa*. Rather, it is understood from the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Purāṇa*, and other sources that the Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa, is denoted by terms such as *Vikhanas* and *Vaikhānasa*. As for example, in the *Khila-śruti*:
[2.17] *khilaśrutau:* (The *Khila-śruti* states:)
It is heard in scripture: “Dhenu is the source of the *vahās*, Aditi of the gods (*suras*), Brahmā of the *ṛbhus*, and Vikhanas of the sages (*munis*).
This is the meaning: Dhenu is the cause of origin for the *vahās*, such as the *ataḍuts* and others; Aditi is the source for the gods, Indra and the rest; and of the *ṛbhus*:
“The Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the Vasus, the Maruts, and likewise the *ṛbhus*... [2.20]
[2.21] “In the same way, the Aṅgirases, the Rudras, and likewise the Ādityas;
[2.22] these eight groups of gods are the lords of the groups of Manvantaras.
[2.23] Thus, among those spoken of by Bhṛgu, Brahmā is the lord of the Sādhyas and others, while Vikhanas is the lord of the Munis—those who are designated by the word ‘Muni’.
[2.24] That Brahmā is denoted by the word *muni* is also understood from the *Mahābhārata*:
[2.25] “Then, having slept through the night, the Blessed One awoke at the end of the night; having awakened, he created the waters and cast his seed into them. [MBh 13, App. 3.265–266] [3.1]
[3.2] That egg became golden, possessing a radiance equal to the thousand-rayed sun;

[3.3] then, through the principle of ego (ahaṅkāra), the Lord, the Sovereign, emitted within it [3.4] Hiraṇyagarbha, the Soul of the Universe, Brahmā, the sage born from the waters. Thus [it is said].
[3.5] The plural form "of the sages" (*munīnām*) is used with the intention of referring to the multiplicity of cosmic eggs (*aṇḍa*). As it is said:
[3.6] "Thousands upon thousands of eggs, and tens of thousands as well; [3.7] of such infinite kinds, there are hundreds of millions of millions."
Thus it is stated in the *Smaraṇa*.
[3.8] If it is asked: "And here, night is the dissolution; where is it understood that it lasts for this long?"
[3.9] In the Mahābhārata: “Four thousand yugas and four hundred yugas—[MBh 13, App. 3.261] [3.10] the Brahmins who perceive reality call this a thousand kalpas. [MBh 13, App. 3.262]
[3.11] “Even ten thousand kalpas are but a single great night for him. [MBh 13, App.
3.263] [3.12–13] If it is asked how the Lord’s designation by the term *Vikhanas* is understood from this scriptural fragment (*khilaśruti*), it is said:
[The meaning of the Veda is to be determined precisely through the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*.]

[3.14] “The Vedic words are difficult to understand because they are scattered, and those that are supplementary (khila) are likewise; therefore, it is by those who know them that these very words, with their clear meanings, are established in the Smṛti-tantra.
[3.15–16] “Even if a twice-born man should know the four Vedas along with the auxiliary sciences and the Upaniṣads...”

“If one does not possess the ancient traditional knowledge (*purāṇa-sad-vidyā*) nor is skilled in the meaning of the Vedas,” and also: “One should augment the Veda with the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*; the Veda is afraid of one who has heard little, thinking, ‘He will deceive me. (MBh 1.1.204)

[3.20–21] On account of this recollection, the determination of the meaning must be made precisely through the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*. In the *Mokṣadharma* section of the *Mahābhārata*, within the hymn of praise by Nārada:

[3.22–23] beginning with “Obeisance to you, O Lord of the gods of gods,” and in the midst of that hymn: “O Teacher of the Phenapas, O Bālakhilya, O Vikhanas, O Vikhanas, O Teacher of the Vaikhānasas, O you of unbroken yoga, O you of unbroken enumeration” [3.24].
In that very same place: “That splendor consisting of the three Vedas which is perceived in him—that is your splendor.”
Those who know the Vedas understand that this Vaikhānasa is the supreme Brahman.
And so it has been said [in the Mahābhārata].
[Etymology of the word *Vikhanaś*] [4.1–2]: Likewise, in the chapter on the Thousand Names, it is recorded in tradition that "Vaikhānasa is the singer of the Sāman."
[The Purpose of the Creation of the World] [4.3] In the *Ātmasaṃhitā* of the *Pañcarātra*:
[4.4] “The world is pervaded by the Great Being, the Real, Vikhanas.”
Go for refuge to that very one, the cause of the world, the infallible.
Thus it was said by Śāṇḍilya with reference to Śatānanda.
In the *Ānandasaṃhitā* of the *Vaikhānasa*:
[4.8] Hari performed the excavation of the investigation into the reality of the Vedānta;
[4.9] they call him by the name Vikhanas, and likewise Vaikhānasa.
Thus it has been stated [ĀS 4.10–12].

Here, by the word "digging" (*khanana*), "volition" (*saṅkalpa*) is meant, according to such scriptural passages as: "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate,' and he performed austerity. Even for the Blessed One, who has attained all desires, there occurs an engagement in the work of creation.

[The Characteristic of Collective Creation] [4.13] Now, regarding the Blessed One, who is distinguished by all auspicious qualities and is a speaker of truth: [4.14] “Of complete sovereignty, heroism, fame, fortune, ...”
[4.15] “And because of his knowledge and dispassion, he is declared to possess the sixfold fortune (bhaga).

[4.16] If it is asked: “For what purpose does he perform creation and so forth, since he is one who is fully endowed with all six qualities and has attained every desire? It is said in reply: [4.17] “He is immeasurable and beyond injunction; wherever he wishes, there he goes, being self-controlled. [MBh 2, App. 21.1605]

[4.18] “The Blessed One rejoices with beings, like a child with toys. [MBh 2, App. 21.1606] [4.19] According to such statements from the *Mahābhārata*, [the Lord acts] solely for the sake of sport (*līlā*).

[4.20] For the purpose of experiencing the sport of creating the world and so forth, after the collective creation (*samaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi*), the Blessed One [proceeds] to the individual creation (*vyaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi*).

[4.21–22] Meditation was performed with regard to the creation of the four-faced Brahmā for the purpose of creating the various distinctions of gods, humans, and so forth. This creation consisting of the conscious and the unconscious is performed by the Blessed Lord; however, the individual (vyaṣṭi) creation is performed by Brahmā. As for what is called the collective (samaṣṭi) creation:
[4.23] “By means of the five elements, the vital breaths, the internal organ, and the ten sense organs...”
[4.24] Those who know the Sāṅkhya treatise recognize twenty-four principles (tattvas).

[5.1] “Great Time (mahākāla), Primordial Matter (pradhāna), Illusion (māyā), Nescience (avidyā), and the Person (puruṣa)—[5.2] thus the authors of the Purāṇas declare; together with these, there are thirty principles. [The characteristic of the individual creation.]

From this statement, it is understood that there is the creation of the principles (*tattva-sṛṣṭi*). By the word "svāntaiḥ" (by their own internal organs), the fourfold internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—namely, "mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and thought (*citta*)"—is denoted. What is called "individual creation" (*vyaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi*) is the creation of the multitude of beings existing within the cosmic egg. [As stated in the scriptures: "The one unborn, red, white, and black," and "The eternal among eternals, the conscious..."

By such scriptural passages as "of volitions," etc., it is taught that the creation of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, which are heard to be eternal, consists in their becoming possessed of gross form and assuming distinct names and forms at the time of creation—after having entered into the Supreme Self—following their state of being unified within the Supreme Self during the period of dissolution in a subtle form and with unmanifest names and forms. [As stated in the texts]: "Having created that... and "That..."
...entered it. Having entered it, it became both *sat* (being) and *tyat* (that)," according to such scriptural passages (*śruti*).
In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"O best of sages, this entire world is thus imperishable and eternal..."
[5.11] “Possessing the conceptual constructions of manifestation and disappearance, of birth and destruction.
[ViṣṇuP] [5.12–13] “Having entered both Prakṛti and Puruṣa by his own will, Hari, at the time of creation having arrived, caused agitation for the sake of dissolution and emergence. [ViṣṇuP]

[5.14] In the Gītās: “Know that both prakṛti and puruṣa are indeed beginningless. [BhGī = MBh 6.35.19ab] [5.15] “The Great Brahman is my womb; in it I place the seed. [5.16] From that, O Bhārata, the birth of all beings occurs. [BhGī = MBh 6.36.3]

And as stated in the manner of [5.17–21], at the time of creation, He joins the "embryo" called consciousness (*cetana*) to that non-sentient entity called *prakṛti*— which is the "Great Brahman" (*mahadbrahma*), the source of the universe. From that conjunction of the sentient and the non-sentient produced thereby, [the world of beings] from the gods down to the immovable [plants] [comes into being].

The origin of all elements occurs when they are not yet mixed. In the same way, the manifestation of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) and so forth, through the mutual conjunction of the fivefold-compounded (*pañcīkṛta*) elements by means of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), is set forth in the *Śrī Viṣṇupurāṇa*. As it says:
[5.22] “Space, wind, fire, water, and likewise earth...”
[5.23] "Endowed with qualities such as sound and so forth, each subsequent one being joined with Brahman;
[5.24] they are remembered as specific manifestations (viśeṣas) because they are calm, terrible, and deluded;
[5.25] possessing diverse potencies and existing separately, they are thus unable to function without a combination. [ViṣṇuP]

[6.1] They were unable to create living beings without coming together in their entirety; [6.2] having come together in mutual conjunction, relying upon one another, [6.3] and having attained complete unity as a single aggregate, they became characterized by a unified whole. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.2.49cd)
[6.4] And because it is presided over by the Puruṣa, as well as through the favor of the Unmanifest (avyakta),
[6.5] those principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas produce the cosmic egg (aṇḍa).
[6.6] That [egg], awakened in due order, is comparable to a bubble upon the water.
[6.7] From the elements, O one of great intelligence, there arose an egg dwelling in the waters;
[6.8] it is the primordial, unsurpassed abode of Viṣṇu, who is of the nature of Brahmā. [6.9] Therein, that Lord of the World, whose true nature is unmanifest, assumes a manifest form.
“Viṣṇu himself is established in the very form of Brahmā. Starting thus, [the text continues]:
“Within that egg was born Brahmā, together with the gods, asuras, and humans. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.2.54)

By these and other passages, the collective creation (*samaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi*) and so forth have been described. Specifically, regarding the individual creation (*vyaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi*), the manner of Brahmā’s birth within the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) and other locations is heard in scripture. For example, in the *Mahopaniṣad*: “Now, therefore, we shall explain the Great Upaniṣad. Verily, there was once Nārāyaṇa alone,” beginning thus, and continuing with “of him... [6.15–21]. In the *Mahopaniṣad*: “Now, therefore, we shall explain the Great Upaniṣad. There was indeed one Nārāyaṇa alone,” starting from this point up to “of him.”

For one who abides within meditation, the sacrifice of praise (yajñastoma) is described. Within that, fourteen persons are born: one daughter; the ten sense organs, with the mind as the eleventh; brilliance as the twelfth; ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*) as the thirteenth; the vital breaths (*praṇa*) as the fourteenth; the self (*ātman*) as the fifteenth; the intellect (*buddhi*); the five elements; the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*); and the five gross elements. He is the one [who completes] the twenty-five.
“The Person. Then, desiring something else, Nārāyaṇa meditated with his mind. As he remained absorbed in meditation, sweat fell from his forehead;
that became these widespread waters.
“Within them was fire;
that fire became a golden egg, and within it, the four-faced Brahmā was born. [This is the manner of Brahmā’s birth from the egg and so forth.]
[6.22] In the *Yajurveda*: "That Prajāpati alone came into being upon the leaf of a lotus. [6.23] In the *Manu-smṛti*: "Thus, in the beginning, he created the waters; into them he cast his seed."
Beginning with [Manu Dharmashastra 1.8cd], [6.24]:

“In him was born Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds,” [Manu Dharmashastra 1.9cd], [7.1]; and in the *Mahābhārata*: “As that god was sleeping, a lotus, radiant as the sun, [arose from his navel].”
[7.2] It issued forth from his navel; Prajāpati was born there.
And thus it is recorded in the Smṛti (MBh 3.194.11).

[7.3–4] If it be asked, "How can the birth of a single being from both the navel and the cosmic egg be logically possible?"—the answer is that this refers to a different *kalpa*. This has been stated in the *Hayaśīrṣa-upākhyāna*:
"[The birth of the one Brahmā from both the navel and the cosmic egg]."
[7.5] “From you my first birth originated, which is honored by the twice-born;
[7.6] indeed, my second ancient birth was that of Cākṣuṣa.”
[7.7] And by your grace, my third birth was the great verbal one;
[7.8] and from you, O Lord, my fourth birth was indeed that of hearing.
[7.9] And my fifth birth from you is said to have been from the nose;
[7.10] and my sixth birth from you was egg-born, produced without a cause.
"But this seventh birth of mine is lotus-born, O Amitaprabha.
[On the fact that the Four-faced One is designated by such terms as *vaikhānasa* and so forth:
[7.12–14] Therefore, [he is the one who is] the sole cause of the great bliss of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the entire universe—the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Brahman.

If it is asked how these [names and forms] are conventionally designated, the answer is true. It is heard in scripture that the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpa-vibhāga*) and so forth was performed by Brahmā from the words of the Veda itself: "By means of the Veda, Prajāpati differentiated names and forms, the existent and the non-existent.

“From the words of the Veda alone, at the beginning, he created the names and forms of beings and their respective functions for the gods and others. [Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.5.63] Manu says: “And he [created] the names and actions of all beings individually. [Manusmṛti 1.21]
"In the beginning, he fashioned the various social orders (*saṃsthā*) from the words of the Veda alone" (Manu Dharmashāstra 1.21).

Since the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpa-vibhāga*) is thus established in both Śruti and Smṛti, the designation "Vaikhānasa" applies only to those who were created by Brahmā in accordance with such Śruti and Smṛti.

Furthermore, just as there is the conventional usage of "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth for those born from the mouth and other parts of the one Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*), and just as those born into lineages (*gotra*) such as Viśvāmitra or Bhāradvāja share the status of adhering to a single *sūtra*; [so it is here].

Without following numerous sūtras, [one might argue] that just as in the case of the *kumuda* (water lily), *kahlāra* (white lotus), and so forth, although they share the commonality of being "born in mud" (*paṅkaja*) according to their etymology, the status of being a "mud-born" (*paṅkaja*)—due to both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*)—applies only to the *tāmarasa* (red lotus); the same applies to the status of being a *vaikhānasa*.
Thus it has been said:

[55.7] "Therefore, the scripture is the authority for you in determining what is to be done and what is not to be done."

[55.8] “Having understood what is prescribed by the ordinances of the scriptures, you ought to perform action here. [MBh 6.38.24] [55.9–12] If it is argued that there is no fault in actions prescribed by the scriptures because of the Lord’s statement, then since the Lord has established that “there is no fault in the enjoyment of my substances and so forth,” there is likewise no fault in the present case either. [Action proceeds] from the word.
"Desisting from speech is indeed the teaching of the learned. Thus, in certain cases, what is dharma becomes adharma, and adharma becomes dharma.
For example:
"When a falsehood has been spoken, if there is the saving of the lives of living beings..."
In that case, the false would be true, and the true would become false.
“In matters concerning women, at weddings, when cattle are being harmed, in cases of oppression, and in the service of a Brahmin, there is no sin in taking an oath.
“If both a Brahmin and a non-Brahmin should come to pose a question, one should answer the Brahmin; for that which one says to a Brahmin is as if one were saying it to oneself.”
And there is a Śruti passage: "He who insults a Brāhmaṇa insults himself; therefore, a Brāhmaṇa is not to be insulted.

And in the Śrautasūtra, it is established: "Everyone greets him in this manner; he does not return the greeting, nor does he offer oblations, except for those that are parts of the Soma sacrifice," and so forth.

[55.22] “In the case of the seizure of all one's property, or when there is danger to life regarding a wife or a prostitute; [55.23] and in a dispute for the sake of cows or Brahmins, there is no sin in taking an oath.”
And there are such traditional texts (*smṛti*) as these.
Furthermore, for those who perform the worship of the Blessed One according to the methods prescribed in the scriptures, there is no fault in the consumption of the substances used therein.
[An investigation into the characteristics of one who acts as a priest for the gods (*devalaka*).]
Furthermore: Is the status of a temple-priest (*devalaka*) determined by birth (*jāti*) or by action (*karman*)?
It cannot be said that it is determined by birth, because it has not been stated as such, and because it is impossible to conceive of it [in that way] through mere whim.
[The state of being a *devalaka* is precisely the performance of unenjoined actions.

[56.3–4] Now, if it is argued that [the term refers to] one who is intent on ritual action (*karmapara*), is this intent on enjoined action (*vihitakarman*) or intent on unenjoined action (*avihitakarman*)?

It is impossible to say that he is devoted solely to prescribed ritual action (*vihitakarman*), for that would entail the consequence that the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Itihāsa*, *Sūtra*, *Purāṇa*, and so forth, would lack authority (*apramāṇya*).
This is because he has not been described as being devoted to the dharma of prescribed rites.
As it is said: "The *Śruti* and *Smṛti* are my very command; he who acts by transgressing them... [56.5–56.6]
“One who violates my command is a traitor to me; even if he is devoted to me, he is not a Vaiṣṇava.

[The faultlessness of worship performed even with another’s property: Thus, because of the fault of violating the Lord’s command, it remains established that [the subject] is one for whom unenjoined action is paramount.
[56.9-10] If it is argued that worship of the Blessed One performed with another’s property, like a sacrifice (*kratu*), serves only the purpose of another—this is not so.
[56.11-12] “A Brahmin devoted to the dharma of another falls and goes to a lower state;
but a Brahmin intent on my ritual action never falls into a low condition anywhere.”
Thus, from the word of the Blessed One.
In another Purāṇa: "Merely by dedicating whatever action one has performed toward oneself..."
“Delighted, he bestows his own state; oh, how great is Hari’s affection!
Furthermore:
[The absence of fault in accepting sacrificial gifts].
“One should give twenty-one *niṣkas* as the teacher’s fee (*ācāryadakṣiṇā*);
the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) shall receive half of that, and the others half of that. Thus is the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) established.
[56.20] But is it not said: "By accepting gifts, the Brahmanic splendor of a Brahmin perishes"?

From the statement of Manu (MDhŚ 4.186cd): “For the spiritual luster (*tejas*) of Brahmins is extinguished by receiving gifts,” and from the statement in the *Anuśāsana-parvan*: “By receiving gifts, the spiritual luster of Brahmins is indeed quenched,” it is recorded in the Smṛti that the destruction of Brahmanic luster occurs through the acceptance of gifts. Furthermore, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for receiving gifts is heard in scripture: “He who officiates at a sacrifice, receives gifts... [text continues].

"Or, having accepted a gift after officiating at a sacrifice, one should recite the Veda three times while fasting; thus one extends the *gāyatrī* verse of the *Sāvitrī* for three nights. A *vara* (boon) is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); by means of the *vara*, one preserves the *vara*, for the self is indeed the *vara*.
[56.25] If it is argued that there is therefore a fault in accepting gifts—the answer is: no.

[The Liberation-bestowing Nature of Remembering Hari] [57.1] "Indeed, other religious duties, even when well-performed, do not provide ultimate protection. [57.2] Yet even my own flawed ritual action protects one from great fear."
Even a heap of evil karma as vast as Mount Meru or Mandara,
upon encountering Keśava as its physician, perishes like a disease of the earth.
Just as one digging for a hidden treasure might obtain the treasure even while seeking only earth out of hatred,
or an ignorant person might obtain it out of desire and fault— so too, by recollecting this, one partakes in liberation.
If even fire, when cast into dry grass by one who hates it or without any effort,
should burn it up, how could Viṣṇu, when worshipped with devotion, not burn away all sins?
"Just as one who is ignorant might become possessed of a vajra-body even while competing with those who drink nectar, so too even one of hostile disposition is surely liberated by remembering Hari.
Thus it is said in the *Nāradīya*: "Even worship performed through hypocrisy, mockery, and the like, delivers people."
[57.12] For one who is compassionate, no other action is ever fruitless; who else is superior to him? [NāradaP.

[57.13–14] Even devotion rendered to you through laughter, disrespect, or deceit grants men the station of Indra—what then need be said of those who are endowed with the quality of goodness (sattva)? [NāradaP.]
[57.15] This very recollection of Hari leads to liberation; it is the inherent nature of things that this is so.
[57.16] Just as the sun is for the destruction of darkness, and fire is for the cooling of cold;
[57.17] even when this recollection of Hari is performed out of anger toward a demon, it serves the same purpose.
[57.18] He brought the Brahmin to a good rebirth along with his followers; how can this be described? [NāradaP.

[57.19–20] Just as when the gods exerted themselves in churning the ocean for the sake of the nectar of immortality, fruits such as the *pārijāta* tree appeared even though they had not been sought. [NāradaP.]
Thus, for those who strive with a single-minded focus on liberation while recollecting the Lord,
divine accomplishments arise— those which are meritorious and followed by further merit.

And in that same work: “For the sake of honoring guests and deities, and specifically for the purpose of maintaining one’s teacher, one may accept gifts from anyone; one does not thereby become defiled by them oneself. (NāradaP 57.23–24)

And because of such a traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*), there is no fault for those engaged in the ritual procedure of worshipping the Blessed One according to the path taught in the scriptures, even when they accept sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) during their respective rites.

[The Worship of the Temple as Supported by the Mahābhārata and Other Texts] Apart from domestic worship (*gṛhārcanā*), the worship of the temple (*ālayārcanā*) is seen to be established in the *Mahābhārata* and other works. For example:
[58.4] In the *Mahābhārata*, in the *Āśvamedhika-parvan*: “How are you worthy of worship? and so forth.
[MBh 14 App. 4.1652pr] [58.5] In the sixth chapter of the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
[58.6] “He who constructs a rampart for the sake of a temple...”
Having attained heaven, he shall become a lord of celestial palaces.
He who constructs a beautiful archway before a temple, whether with stone or even with wood, shall become a lord of heaven.
[Viṣṇudharmottara.P 58.10–11] But he who should construct a temple for Viṣṇu out of wood, stone,
or clay, or even one fashioned from bricks, his reward shall be great.
That man who causes a pavilion for Viṣṇu to be constructed obtains the merit of performing thousands of horse-sacrifices day after day.
He attains that imperishable world of Keśava;
for the sake of an image of Mahāviṣṇu, he should prepare an excellent stone.
For sixty thousand years, he is honored in the world of heaven.
Thus [it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara-purāṇa, 58.17–19].

Furthermore, the impossibility of these—such as the walls, gateways, pavilions, images, and stone-work—possessing their own domestic deities (*gṛhadevatā*) is established in the Śrīvaikhānasa-saṃhitās. In this context, the greatness of the worshipper (*arcaka-māhātmya*) is discussed incidentally.
In the *Bṛhannāradīya*:
"Once that great sinner was like Death itself to living beings."
Beginning with [BṛhannāradaP 58.21] and continuing through [58.22]:
“In the middle of his grove stood a beautiful temple of Keśava.”
Seeing it covered with golden armor, the hunter went away with joy.
"I shall take away many gold pieces from here," he resolved;
and that miser, greedy for theft, went to the abode of Viṣṇu.
There he saw the best of the twice-born, Udanka, who was peaceful, skilled in the meaning of reality,
devoted to the service of Viṣṇu, and a treasure-house of austerities.
[59.3] Seeing him— devoted to solitude, compassionate, free from desire, and eager for meditation— the hunter considered him an obstacle to his own purpose. [59.4]
[BrhannaradaP] [59.5] At night, he intended to take away the various articles belonging to the deity.

Having stated, through such passages as [BṛhannāradaP 59.6–7], the existence of a separate temple and its attendant priest, and having further established that even his death would result from his engagement in harming the priest— an act which obstructed his own purpose—
[the text proceeds with] the *Viṣṇupādodakamāhātmyam*.
[59.8] Seeing that the hunter had fallen, the great sage Udaṅka, filled with compassion, [59.9] sprinkled him with the water from Viṣṇu’s feet.
[59.10] Having touched the water from Hari’s feet, the hunter was freed from defilement;
[59.11] ascending a divine celestial chariot, he then spoke to this Sage:
[59.12] Thus, the majesty of the Blessed One’s foot-water is established.
In that very same work— the dialogue between Yajñadhvaja and Vītihotra [concerning the fruit of placing a lamp in the *ālaya*]:
“Once, blinded by desire and wishing to take pleasure with another’s wife...”
At night, he arrived at a temple of Viṣṇu that was empty, having been worshipped with offerings and the like.
There, O Brahmin, for the sake of enjoying sensual pleasures, that lustful man wiped that spot with the hem of his own garment while lying down.
[59.18] As many particles of dust as were swept away by him at that time,
[59.19] so much evil committed in previous births was destroyed right then.
[59.20] A lamp was placed there for the sake of sexual pleasure, O best of the twice-born;
by that act as well, his evil karma came to a complete end.
If even one who has performed this rite involuntarily has attained such success,
how much more so for those who are devoted and tranquil through correct worship?

[The Fruit of Circumambulating Ālaya] [60.1] Therefore, listen, O best of Brahmins: the imperishable Lord Nārāyaṇa [60.2] grants liberation to his worshippers, whether through knowledge or even through ignorance.
Likewise, in that very same work, in the dialogue between Indra and Sudharmā:
“O Śakra, in the past I was a vulture due to the remnants of my evil karma; I remained upon a patch of ground, feeding on impure flesh.”
[60.6] Once, O Lord, while I was staying on the rampart of Viṣṇu’s palace,
[60.7] I was struck by a hunter’s weapon in the evening as I was entering Viṣṇu’s palace.
[60.8] While my life-breath was at my throat, a certain dog, greedy for flesh,
[60.9] seized me with its own mouth as it was being pursued by other dogs.
Having performed a circumambulation of that temple of the Lord Viṣṇu,
the inner self, which pervades the universe, attained satisfaction through that very act.
He bestowed the supreme state upon both me and the dog;
such is the fruit corresponding to one who has performed a circumambulation.
"But since I have attained this, O Śakra, how much more so from perfect worship?
Those who always worship the healthy Nārāyaṇa with devotion—the hosts of deities, including Brahmā and the other gods, worship them. Thus it is said.
[The five impure things] [60.17]:
Thus it is said in the *Aśvamedhika* [Parvan]: “In this world, O Bhārata, there are three things that are unholy and five things that are impure. [MBh 13, App. 4.3249]
[60.18] “A dog, a Śūdra, and a dog-cooker (śvapāka), O Pāṇḍava—these three are impure.
[60.19] A temple-priest, a cock, a sacrificial post, a menstruating woman, and the husband of a low-caste woman—[60.20] these five are unclean. Thus it is said.
[Those Unqualified for Worshiping the Blessed One, etc.
[60.21] In the *Śrīvaikhānasa*: “Outcastes such as Sūtas born of inverse unions, heretics, and likewise those who have fallen from their caste;”
Nihilists who have broken the bounds of propriety, as well as those who revile the Vedas.
Those afflicted with malignant diseases, as well as those who revile their gurus,
are not worthy even to behold the worship of the God of gods or the offering of oblations; therefore, one should keep the door covered with a curtain.

Because it has been established thus, superiority is not possible for those base individuals (such as *devalakas*) who lack the fitness for worshipping or beholding the Blessed One. [The superiority of those who sacrifice to the Blessed One without intermediaries.]

Those for whom the right to worship the Lord directly (*advāraka-bhagavad-yajana*) is prescribed in the *Kalpasūtras* according to the methods stated in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Purāṇas*, and so forth, should be known as superior. As the *Śruti* says:
"As one's resolve (*kratu*) is in this world, so it becomes after departing from here.
And the *Smṛti*: "By the very path declared in the Veda, [one attains Him] who dwells in the hearts of all beings..."
Those devotees who worship me attain union with me.
Therefore, as long as a person lives, they should worship Hari;
such a mortal is not stained by sins and shall attain the abode of Hari.
[61.11] Those who constantly worship Viṣṇu are the eternal purifiers of the world;
[61.12] whether they are of evil conduct or of good conduct, they are especially worthy of worship.
[The state of being objects of the Blessed One’s affection for the Vaikhānasas]

[61.13-16] Furthermore, in the *Anuśāsana-parvan* (chapter 90), during the discussion on worthy recipients (*pātra*), Vyāsa established the unworthiness of the *devalakas* and the worthiness of those devoted to virtuous deeds.
To reinforce his own statement, he cited the fact that "the Vaikhānasa sages were dear to Indra," thereby referring to those who are objects of the Lord's affection.

It has been established that the statement of the Vaikhānasas is also heard, as follows: “O Yudhiṣṭhira, those who constantly observe the covenant of the ṛṣis, being resolute and knowing all dharmas—the gods know them to be Brāhmaṇas. (MBh 13.9.42)

[61.19] O Bhārata, you should know that there are sages devoted to the study of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*), as well as those devoted to knowledge (*jñāna*), those devoted to austerity (*tapas*), and those devoted to ritual action (*karman*). [61.20–21] O Bhārata,
the offerings to the ancestors (*kavya*) should be presented to those who are devoted to knowledge.
[61.22] In that regard, those Brāhmaṇas who do not criticize anyone are the best.
[61.23] But as for those who criticize others in their talk, one should not feed them at *śrāddha* ceremonies.
[61.24] O King, Brāhmaṇas who are reviled can destroy a family for three generations. (MBh 13.9.44–45)
[62.1] O King, the words of the Vaikhānasa sages are heard:
[62.2] One should examine from afar those Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas; [62.3] whether they be dear or even hateful, one should offer that śrāddha to them. (MBh 13.9.46)
“O Bhārata, a single man who knows the mantras and is purified by them is worth more than a man who might feed a thousand times a thousand who are ignorant of the *ṛc*s.
[MBh 13.9.47] [The greatness of those devoted to the recitation of mantras such as the eight-syllabled one.]

[62.6–7] Thus, it is stated in the Purāṇas that even a killer of a Brāhmaṇa is purified by the sight of those who are devoted to the recitation of mantras such as the *Puruṣasūkta*, consisting of eight or twelve syllables.
As it says in the *Padmapurāṇa*:
“Together with its limbs, its mantras, its ritual applications (*nyāsa*), and its respective *ṛc*-verses, meters, and presiding deities...”

“Those supreme among men who recite the twelve-syllable mantra, along with its ritual of initiation (*dīkṣā*), its meditation (*dhyāna*), and its yantra, as well as the Lord of Mantras consisting of eight syllables—
even a slayer of a Brahmin would be purified by seeing them, let alone a Vaiṣṇava himself. [PadmaP]

It is also heard: "Whoever indeed studies the eight-syllabled word of Nārāyaṇa without omitting any part, he reaches a full lifespan; he obtains the prosperity of Prajāpati, the abundance of wealth, and lordship over cattle; from that, he attains immortality—yes, from that he attains immortality."
In the *Śrīpāñcarātra*, within the *Kapiñjalasaṃhitā*:
“One who is engaged in officiating at sacrifices and teaching, who bestows grace upon disciples, and who is devoted to the *mantras* and *tantras*, is to be known as an *ācārya*. (*KapiñjalaS*)
Whether in a hermitage or even in the forest, he is called a *vaikhānasa*;
one who dwells in the forest should avoid all worldly customs.
Thus [it is said]. In the *Yama-smṛti*:
"The mortal who, out of greed for wealth, has killed a learned twice-born man..."
[62.21] “He should recite the *Puruṣasūkta*; staying in water, he should meditate on Hari.

[62.22–24] If it is argued that such powers are heard of even for those devoted solely to the recitation (*japa*) of the eight-syllable mantra, then [the same applies] to the primary practitioners and others who perform the direct worship of the Lord by means of those very mantras prescribed in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*.
By whom can the preeminence of the Vaikhānasas—which is established through the logic of the "how much more so" (*kaimutikanyāya*)—be refuted?
[Definition of the Devalakas] Furthermore: just as the origin and other details concerning the Vaikhānasas are specifically described in the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and so forth...
If it were established that others are specifically established in that same way, then there would be equality between them and the Vaikhānasas;
however, such is not seen.
Now, let us examine who these *devalakas* actually are.
In the *Vaikhānasa* [tradition]:
"A Brahmin who is not a Vaikhānasa, yet worships Hari in a temple, is indeed called a *devalaka*; he is excluded from offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*)."
Born into the lineage of the Vaikhānasas and initiated according to the Pāñcarātra,
he neither performed initiation nor was truly born [into the tradition],
yet out of greed and delusion, he offered worship to me.
"But if he performs it especially for his own benefit, he would become a *devalaka*.
[Regarding the *devalaka*, see the *Traividyasamāmnāya*.
In the *Saṃkarṣaṇasaṃhitā* of the *Pāñcarātra*:

“Some are temple-priests by profession (*karmadevalaka*), others are temple-priests for a ritual period (*kalpadevalaka*), and still others are pure temple-priests (*śuddhadevalaka*); thus, temple-priests are said to be of three kinds.”
[The Saṅkarṣaṇasaṃhitā.
[The Characteristics of the Ritual Priest and the Temple Priest. [63.12] He who, seeking wealth and observing the proper time, worships the deity—he indeed [is the temple priest].
One who is excluded from all ritual acts is called a *karmadevalaka*.
[From the *Saṅkarṣaṇasaṃhitā*:
A priest who knows the rules of the *Pāñcarātra* but is devoid of initiation is remembered as a *kalpadevalaka*, even if he possesses the authority of one learned in the four Vedas.
[From the Saṅkarṣaṇasaṃhitā:
One who knows the procedures taught in the Āgamas and subsists upon Bhadrakālī is declared to be a pure *devalaka*, excluded from all ritual acts.
[From the *Saṅkarṣaṇasaṃhitā*] [63.18] Divinity does not exist according to the injunctions spoken by the Ṛṣis;
[63.19] therefore, with every effort, one should worship according to the Vedic method alone.
Thus [in the Saṅkarṣaṇasaṃhitā 63.20]. In the Śivaśekhara-tantra, Rudra says [63.21]:
“Now I shall speak of the temple-priests (devalakas); listen, O Goddess, with a concentrated mind.”
Some are deities by virtue of their karma; others are deities for the duration of an eon.
[Śivaśekharatantra] [63.23] But others are the pure *devalakas*; thus the *devalakas* are remembered as being of three kinds.
[63.24] He who performs the annual worship according to the path taught in other sūtras—
[Śivaśekharatantra] [The Characteristics of the Ritual Devas]:
[64.1] One who is uninitiated [into the Śaiva system] but performs rituals in the tantra is a *karmadevalaka*.
O Daughter of the Mountain, by this very method, one who worships for three years is certainly declared to be a *kalpadevalaka*.
[Śivaśekharatantra] [The Characteristics of a Pure Devalaka] [64.4] And he who has heard the Āgama without being authorized by his preceptor;
In terms of moral conduct, both his disciples, Śuddha and Devalaka, were likewise.
[Śivaśekharatantra] [The threefold nature of being a temple-priest (*devalaka*) pertains to the domain of Rudra and others] [64.6]:
"The threefold status of being a *devalaka* never pertains to Viṣṇu."
[64.7] This is accepted by the scriptures as having Rudrakālī and others as its objects.
Thus it is stated in another Smṛti, the *Śivaśekharatantra* (64.8):
“Śarva, Sūrya, as well as Candra, Durgā, and the other deities of Rudra...”
That man who worships with a wager falls immediately.
Durgā, Bhadrakālī, the Buddha, Kṣetrapālaka,
and Pañcapūjā— these are known as the five devalakas.
“[The worship of] Āditya, Ambikā, Viṣṇu, Gaṇanātha, and Maheśvara at home— these are remembered as the five *devālakas*,” so it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
“Those who are indeed worshippers of Caṇḍikā, Durgā, Jyeṣṭhā, Bhairava, and Rudra are known as *devalakas*.”

Thus [ViṣṇudharmottaraP 64.16], Viṣṇu says: “Even a Brahmin who upholds the four Vedas, if he is intent on the worship of the gods for the sake of another out of a desire for wealth, he would be equal to a Caṇḍāla. [ViṣṇuP 64.17]

[64.18–19] Thus, by these statements, it is clearly understood that, according to a path not approved by the Teacher, the status of being a *devalaka* (one who serves as a priest for hire) is established for both those who worship [the Buddha] and those who worship other deities.
[64.20] Furthermore: “Virtue (*dharma*) is declared to be the Bull (*vṛṣa*); he who causes its destruction, the gods know him as a *vṛṣala*, more base even than a dog-cooker (*śvapaca*). [64.21]
[The Etymology of the Word *Devalaka*] (64.22–65.2): Just as the word *vṛṣala* is derived in the sense of one who obstructs the path taught in the Vedas and scriptures,

so too the word *devalaka* [is derived from the root] *div*, which [in the Dhatupatha] means "to play, to desire victory, to transact, to shine, to praise, to rejoice, to intoxicate, to sleep, to love, and to go."

Thus, according to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), since it is composed of the root *div*—which signifies "path" as a synonym for "going"—it can be etymologically derived as that which leads to the attainment of the "laya" (dissolution) of the path taught in the Vedas; consequently, it does not apply in its entirety to the Vaikhānasas, who are opposed to that [Vedic path] and are instead established in the Vedic way. And so it is said:

Hārīta says: "Those Brahmins who are forest-dwellers (*vaikhānasa*) and devoted to the worship of Hari are not called temple-priests (*devalaka*), because they take refuge at the lotus feet of Viṣṇu."
Thus, in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*: “[The absence of the designation ‘devalaka’ for the *vaikhānasa*s]” (Vṛddhahārīta 8.78) [65.5].
Atri says:
“One who, free from hypocrisy and greed, worships Viṣṇu with devotion according to the Vedic ritual alone—he indeed is not a *devalaka*. Thus it is said.

Otherwise, if those who worship a temple were considered *devalakas* (temple-priests) even when following the path taught in the Śruti, then the statements in the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and other texts that prescribe such temple worship would be rendered meaningless.

If it is objected: "If even the worship of the Lord performed out of ignorance bestows liberation, why should that same worship not bestow liberation even when performed by one who lacks qualification and acts without the authority of the scriptures?
The answer is no. For that would result in the transgression of the Lord’s command.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
“He who, casting aside the rules of the scriptures, acts according to his own whims, attains neither success, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal. (MBh 6.38.23)

“‘The Śruti and Smṛti are my very command; he who acts by transgressing them is a violator of my command and a traitor to me. Even if he be my devotee, he is certainly not a Vaiṣṇava. Thus [it is said]: ‘And this is dear to me, Viṣṇu, the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.’”

“A human being should not transgress Vedic conduct even in thought. Thus, that which is performed by one who lacks the qualification is not in accordance with the scriptures; therefore, even if it is performed according to the methods taught in the Tantras, it does not bestow liberation.
Now, [one might object]: “By Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have received the initiatory marks...”
[65.20] “Mādhava is to be honored, served, and worshipped—
he who was sung of by Saṅkarṣaṇa while adhering to the Sāttvata rite.
[The lack of capacity for granting liberation in worship according to the Tantras]

It is replied: "One who has received initiation in one among the four types of Tantras has no eligibility for another Tantra."
“First is the Mantra-siddhānta, and second is that called Āgama;
third is the Tantra-siddhānta, and beyond that is the Tantra-antara doctrine.”

[PadmaS Caryāpāda 19.113ab] [66.3] Thus, among the fourfold systems of established doctrine (siddhānta), [66.4] “O best of the twice-born, one who has been initiated into a single tantra or established doctrine...”

[Padma Sūtra, Caryāpāda 19.131] [66.6–7] The office of a teacher, the role of a priest, and the worship of the Enemy of Madhu—

If it is asked, "In that case, what is the interpretation of the statement from the *Mahābhārata* beginning with 'by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas'?"—it is replied:
The followers of Mādhava say: He is to be worshipped by Brāhmaṇas who have been defined as having the primary qualification for the direct (*advāraka*) worship of the Lord;

"...by Śūdras, by women, and likewise by others;
Hari, the Lord of All, is always to be worshipped and served according to their respective fitness.
Thus, from the words of Bhāradvāja: "Worship is said to extend up to the *arghya* offering, and adoration extends up to the *havis* oblation."
This is because [the text] demonstrates that *arcana* and *pūjana* have distinct meanings;

Otherwise, if one were to admit the eligibility of even a *śūdra* for worship, *arcana*, and so forth, there would be a contradiction with the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Sūtra*, *Purāṇa*, and other authorities.

[67.23–25] These statements also establish that the Śūdra lacks the qualification [for Vedic rites]. The Śruti says: “Therefore, the Śūdra is not entitled to sacrifice. For he was created after the deities; therefore, the Śūdra, though possessing many cattle, is unfit for sacrifice among the gods.

[69.1] Therefore, a Śūdra who is overwhelmed by the quality of darkness (tamas) has no entitlement whatsoever to the worship of the Blessed Lord.

[69.2–7] If it be argued that they might have an entitlement to the propitiation of the Blessed Lord in the manner taught by Śaunaka and others—that is incorrect. For in those cases, there is no specification of a particular qualified person; and even though it is stated in a general sense, in the Śruti, Smṛti, Sūtras, Purāṇas, Mahābhārata, Vaikhānasa, Pāñcarātra, Śaiva, Śilpa, Jyotiṣa, and other such texts...

Since [the practice] has been specifically established for qualified practitioners, it is logical that the procedure for worship taught by Śaunaka and others also culminates in this very [text], by virtue of the principle of all Vedic branches having a single purport (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*), the principle of the general and the particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-nyāya*), the principle that "everything studied within my section is for my sake," the similarity of context (*prakaraṇa-sāmya*), and the principle of the combination of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra-nyāya*) due to the identity of the deity to be worshipped.

If it is asked how this applies to the followers of other sūtras: the fruit of propitiating the Blessed One is accomplished simply by performing the duties of one's own stage of life (*āśrama*). As it is stated in the *Smṛtis*: "Whether much or little, whatever ritual action is enjoined for someone according to their own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, when that much of the purpose of the scripture has been performed, everything has been performed."

“Those who sacrifice to the ancestors, the gods, the brahmins, and the sacrificial fire—

[69.20] Having risen in the morning and bathed according to the rules, always composed in mind, one should worship Viṣṇu—who is designated by such names as Deva and others—by means of those various rites.

The Blessed One alone is to be propitiated by means of the eternal Vedic dharmas.
[Śāṇḍilyasmṛti] [70.3] He alone is to be worshipped in every way; there is no other who delivers one from saṃsāra.

"O lord of men, whatever dharma has been ordained for each person by the Self-Existent One... [MBh 14, App. 4.222].

4.223] In the *Padma Purāṇa*: “Those Vaiśyas who here protect their own duties as prescribed by the scriptures and the duties of their caste in their entirety, do not go to the abode of Yama. [PadmaP]

In another *Smṛti*: "One who desires the highest good in this world should always diligently resort to his own specific duty (*svadharma*), consisting of action prescribed by the *Śruti*, the *Smṛti*, and the conduct of the virtuous."

“The path leading to the goal is none other,” and “The Brahmins seek [the Self] through sacrifice, through charity, through austerity, and through fasting”—these scriptural passages confirm this meaning. Therefore, it is impossible for anyone to attain equality with the venerable followers of the Vaikhānasa-sūtras, who are authorized to worship the Lord without [other] intermediaries; enough of this prolixity. "Just as Vikhanas is declared to be the primordial source of the Munis,

Thus, in the ancient scripture [the *Brahmakaivarta Purāṇa*], Bhṛgu said:

Those who know the Vedas understand them to be the Vaikhānasa branch.
Beginning with this, the *Purātantra* states:
“This is indeed the supreme Vaiṣṇava thread that brings about all accomplishments;
for it is the first of all threads, and because it belongs to Viṣṇu, it is truly so. (*Purātantra* 71.7–8)
In that same way, it was followed by me and by Kāśyapa and the other [disciples].
And in the *Skanda-purāṇa* [Purātantra 71.10]: “The supreme Creator, the Lotus-born, assigned the great branch of the Vaikhānasas to his own Sūtra; therein he established the threefold propitiation.”
[71.12] “He has spoken of the conduct of those who know the meaning of the Vedas (*nigama*) in its various divisions.

[71.16] “First, for the sake of the world, the powerful Pacana was created from my mouth. [MBh 14, App.

Furthermore, in the *Navagrahamakha*, the circularity of the solar disc (*savitṛmaṇḍala*) is stated in the Sūtra by such passages as "square, circular," and so forth.

For example, in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
“Viśvakarman indeed performed the pacification of his brilliance;

In accordance with that, Bodhāyana and others have stated that the solar disc is circular in shape, whereas previously it was described as square; this very point is established in the present sūtra.

Thus, having recalled the *Vaikhānasa-sūtra* which states, "The forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) who follows the conduct prescribed by the *Vaikhānasa-śāstra* is a *vaikhānasa*," Bodhāyana sets forth the duties of the third stage of life (*āśrama*).

Likewise, in the *Āgnivaiśya-sūtra*: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the enumeration of the Sūtras. Bodhāyana, Āpastamba, Satyāṣāḍha, Drāhyāyaṇa, Āgastya, Śākalya, Āśvalāyana, Śāmbhavīya, and Kātyāyana—these are the nine earlier Sūtras. Vaikhānasa, Śaunakīya, Bhāradvāja, Āgnivaiśya, and Jaiminīya..."

The Vādhūla, Mādhyandina, Hiraṇyakeśīya, and Kauṣītaka—these are the nine later Sūtras. Thus there are eighteen Sūtras and eighteen authors of Sūtras. These are rooted in the four Vedas. The earlier Sūtras are bodily (śārīra) and general (sāmānya), while the later Sūtras, such as those of the Vaikhānasa and others, are related to Viṣṇu and are divine (daivika). Such is the primacy of the Vaikhānasa Sūtra.
And its status as Vaiṣṇava is also stated.
Furthermore, the superiority of this Sūtra has already been established previously by the passage beginning with, "Those twice-born who have been consecrated by the Vaikhānasa-sūtra.

Therefore, it is proven that this Sūtra is the first of all Sūtras. Consequently, its status as the most excellent of all Sūtras is also logically justified; thus, the second reason has been demonstrated.
[72.22] Thus ends the examination of the second reason. [The examination of the third reason:
the *Vaikhānasa-sūtra*’s conformity with the path of the Vedas.]

[73.1-3] Now, in order to demonstrate that this *Śrīvaikhānasa-sūtra* possesses a basis in direct revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), which distinguishes it from other *sūtras*, the third reason is set forth: "because in all ritual acts it follows the path of the revealed texts. To explain:
[The scriptural authority of the rule for pure sipping of water (*śuddhācamana*)].

[73.4–9] Regarding the procedure for pure *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water), the *sūtra* prescribes pure *ācamana* with the words "May the *Ṛgveda* be pleased," and so forth, in accordance with the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) which states: "In that he sips water three times, thereby he pleases the *ṛc*s," and so on. If it is objected that Bodhāyana has also stated the procedure for pure *ācamana*, this is true; however, beginning with the words "We shall explain the procedure for *ācamana*," he continues: "One should sip water three times with the hands joined like the ears of a cow."

It has been stated that through the act of sipping water (*ācamana*), there is satisfaction of the *Ṛgveda* and the other Vedas: "By what he drinks first, he gratifies the *Ṛgveda*; by what he drinks second, the *Yajurveda*; by what he drinks third, he gratifies the *Sāmaveda*. However, this is not a *mantra*. Herein, the principal elements of the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*) as prescribed by the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Sūtra*—namely, the offering of the *arghya* and so forth—are set forth; beginning with the words "In the morning, [saying] 'Sūryaś ca'... and having performed the sipping of water (*ācamya*).

“Having sprinkled [water] with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, having consecrated the water with the *gāyatrī* mantra, and having scattered it while facing the sun, he performs a circumambulation,” and so forth.

If it is argued that the procedure for the twilight worship (*sandhyāvandana*) was also stated by Bodhāyana, this is not so; for [he says]: “Now, therefore, the procedure for the twilight worship... [etc.]

We shall now explain this. Having gone to the water’s edge, one who is already pure, or one who has been consecrated by bathing, or one who is not yet consecrated, having washed his feet and hands and sipped water (ācamana), sprinkles himself with water that is fragrant, or with waters accompanied by mantras addressed to the Waters (vāruṇī), those of golden color (hiraṇyavarṇā), those of purifying power (pāvamānī), the Vyāhṛtis, and other purificatory formulas; thus he becomes pure. Moreover, they cite this example: [BaudhDhS 2.4.7.1–3]
“Immersing oneself in water for bathing is prescribed for all castes;
for the twice-born, however, sprinkling with water accompanied by mantras remains as their duty. Thus [BaudhDhS 2.4.7.3–2].
And at the commencement of all ritual acts, prior to the time for the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), one should purify oneself with this very collection of purifiers.

Having sprinkled himself, he becomes pure. Now they also quote: "Seated upon *darbha* grass, holding *darbha* grass, with water in his hand, facing westward, one should repeat the *Sāvitrī* a thousand times; or a hundred times by means of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Then, by means of three breath-controls..."

"By means of the *brahmahṛdaya* and the two *vāruṇī* verses, he worships the night," and so forth; thus the ritual cleansing (*mārjana*) and other such acts are mentioned, while the principal acts, such as the offering of the *arghya*, are not mentioned. [BaudhDhS 2.4.7.4–9] [The method of the *brahmayajña* as taught in the Śruti] [The selection of the Soma preceded by the selection of the Brahman priest]

[74.4–9] The Brahmayajña. In the *Talavakāropaniṣad*: "Of that [Gāyatrī], this is indeed the first quarter: ‘Oṃ bhūḥ, that excellent splendor of Savitṛ; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, we meditate upon the radiance of the divine; Oṃ suvaḥ, may he impel our thoughts’—thus foot by foot. ‘Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ, that excellent splendor of Savitṛ, we meditate upon the radiance of the divine; Oṃ suvaḥ, may he impel our thoughts’—thus half-verse by half-verse."

"Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ; may we meditate upon that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ, who shall inspire our thoughts"—having thus recited the Sāvitrī in its entirety as prescribed, it is likewise stated here in this Sūtra.

In the rites beginning with the Āghāra offerings, everything is performed according to the Śrauta ritual. Here, after the selection of the Brahman priest, the selection of Soma is also mentioned: "Soma is the king of us Brāhmaṇas—[those] whose king is Soma."
"Regarding the statement, 'The Brāhmaṇas':

Viṣṇu and Soma, as Brahmā, spoke first; Viṣṇu said, 'I am the foundation of the Brāhmaṇas,' and Soma said, 'I am the foundation. They both approached Prajāpati with this question, and Prajāpati said:"
"The Vedas go to Viṣṇu,
and the lunar mansions go to Soma; both of them are devoted to Brahman," he said.

"Since you two are worshipped when worshipping, praised when praising, beloved when being beloved, devoted to Brahman and knowers of Brahman, and the very foundation of the Brāhmaṇas—therefore, whatever they shall declare concerning me in the sacrifices through the Veda, that shall be I," so said Viṣṇu. "Therefore, Viṣṇu is the sacrifice and the foundation of the Brāhmaṇas. And it is known from scripture: [74.15–17] *pūjitau pūjayantau stutau stunvantau priyau priyavantau brahmaṇyau brahmavittau brāhmaṇānāṃ pratiṣṭhātārau bhavata iti yan māṃ brahmaṇā vakṣyanti yajñeṣu so 'ham iti viṣṇur abravīt. tasmād viṣṇur yajño brāhmaṇānāṃ pratiṣṭhā iti. vijñāyate ca.*

"Because of this Brāhmaṇa passage, 'The Brāhmaṇas are indeed the *chandāṃsi*,' he said, 'Wherever the Brāhmaṇas shall declare me among the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), there I shall be. Therefore, Soma is the king of the Brāhmaṇas; and thus it is known from the Brāhmaṇa that the twenty-eighth [mansion] belongs to the Brāhmaṇas, and his word is meritorious. Both of these are devoted to the Brahman."

This is because it is well-known from the Śruti: "The two knowers of Brahman are the establishers of the Brāhmaṇas; they are established among the Brāhmaṇas. He who performs rituals preceded by Brāhmaṇas acts for the success of the sacrifice.

Thus, in this context, since the sacrifice to the nine planets (navagrahamakha) is the primary rite among the rites for pacification (śāntika), prosperity (pauṣṭika), and so forth, the procedure for the five fire-pits (pañcāgnikuṇḍa) is prescribed.

It has been said: "Now we shall explain the pacification of the planets (*grahaśānti*). The course of worldly affairs depends upon the planets; therefore, when something adverse befalls oneself, one should properly worship the planets. [The Preeminence of *Grahaśānti*]

If it is asked how the pacification of planetary afflictions (*grahaśānti*) holds such preeminence, it is said: “A learned Brahmin, meditating upon and performing rites for the sun as it rises and sets, attains all that is auspicious; ‘This sun is Brahman’—being Brahman already, he reaches Brahman, he who knows thus. Thus, with the intention that this very [rite] is the worship of the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa residing in the center of the solar orb— as established by such scriptural statements as “He who rises burning,” “He effects the abiding of Viṣṇu’s power in the eternal sun,” and “The object of meditation is always situated in the middle of the solar disc”— the authors of the Sūtras [have prescribed] this grahayajña.
Its preeminence has been stated. Likewise, at the end it is also said: "Otherwise, a much greater fault occurs.
And Bodhāyana says:
"Now, therefore, we shall explain the rites of the cups, the guest-offering, the bali-oblation, and the upahāra-offerings."
[The Savitṛ-homa]:
[75.10] The planets clearly lead a man who lacks faith, who is impure, who does not recite prayers, and who has abandoned auspicious rites, to the abode of Yama. [75.11]

And having first stated the precedence of the planets for all rites among the planets, and having therein taught the procedure for the five sacrificial fire-pits (*pañcāgnikuṇḍavidhāna*), the oblation to Savitṛ in the form of Viṣṇu in the *sabhya* fire is established by the statement: “In the *sabhya* [fire], [the oblation is] to Savitṛ.
[75.23–24] Thus: “Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman”; “Brahman alone is the eldest of beings, so who is worthy to rival him?”; “Agni indeed is the lowest of the gods, Viṣṇu the highest.”

[76.2–3] Having thus described the method of propitiation—which is not mentioned in other sūtras—by way of Nārāyaṇa being the supreme, he has also stated therein the arrangement of the five forms (pañcamūrti) in accordance with such scriptural passages as, “This very Person is fivefold, consisting of five selves. [76.4–5] It was already stated previously that in the case of the Āghāra offerings and so forth, it is established by direct perception that they are performed exactly as prescribed in the Śruti. “Having examined all this in its entirety with the eye of knowledge,
the wise man should indeed abide in his own duty (svadharma) on the authority of the Śruti.
[Manu Dharmashāstra 2.8] In the Śrī Bhārata:
“Dharma is indeed that which is established by the Veda; adharma is its opposite.

We have heard that the Veda is Nārāyaṇa himself, the self-existent. [MBh 12.231.13–14] Pracetas said: “Those who follow external scriptures and others who are devoid of the Veda are full of darkness.”
[76.15] “Whatever they might say, one should not do that; dharma is ordained from the Veda.

"The second is from the treatises on Dharma, and the third is for the sake of gathering the world. [MBh 14 App.
