[76.21] Thus concludes the examination of the third reason. [Examination of the fourth reason] [The Vaikhānasa Sūtra’s status as a manual teaching all ritual actions accompanied by mantras]

[77.1–2] Now, first of all, in order to demonstrate that through the performance of the duties prescribed in the *Vaikhānasa-sūtra* there is the attainment of infinite and stable fruit, as well as birth in a noble family and an abundance of results, the fourth reason is set forth: "because it teaches all ritual actions accompanied by mantras. It is as follows:

In this *sūtra*, regarding the rules for the daily performance (*nityānuṣṭhāna*), the acts beginning with the washing of the hands and so forth are prescribed as being accompanied by mantras, starting from the words "I am Indra, by both [hands]. In the *brahmayajña*, there is a specific variation beginning with "The cosmic order (*ṛta*) and truth (*satya*)," and so on. In the rite for an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), the accompaniment of mantras is explicit. In other *sūtras*, the procedure for the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) for the domestic fire (*aupāsana*) which was not mentioned there is set forth. Regarding the rule for the pouring of clarified butter (*āghāra*):

The fact that [the rites] are accompanied by mantras is established. It is the same in the case of the internal oblation (*antahoma*). In bodily consecrations (*saṃskāra*) such as the initiation (*upanayana*), which are preceded by the *nāndīmukha* rite, the accompaniment of mantras is directly perceived. Regarding the *sthālīpāka* and other [rites], the phrase "as before" provides a concise exposition of the procedure for the *āghāra* offering—which was previously explained in detail—for the sake of ease of performance.

[The presence of mantras even in other rites] [77.11–15]: Even in other rites, there is the presence of mantras. In that regard, having raised the objection himself that because it is stated in some cases to be "silently" (*tūṣṇīm*), there is no presence of mantras, he established the presence of mantras by means of another method.
It is understood that in various instances, even where there is an absence of suitability for mantras, there is nevertheless the presence of mantras in every prescribed domain.

Since other sūtras do not mention the use of mantras even in those prescribed domains, it follows that those [sūtras] do not require mantras for all ritual actions. In that regard, one observes an independence from other sūtras even with respect to other ritual actions.

[77.16–19] By Bodhāyana, the throwing of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the spreading of the sacrificial grass (*paristaraṇa*) in the rites beginning with the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*) was prescribed as being entirely silent (*tūṣṇīm*).

If it is asked, "What is the distinction when actions are stated to be accompanied by mantras?"—it is replied: When actions possess mantras, they are indeed more powerful; through the propitiation of the Lord who is the object of the ritual, there is the attainment of infinite and stable fruits, as well as birth into a noble family.

And it is understood from the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and other sources that [rites performed with knowledge are more effective]. For example, regarding the fact that actions accompanied by mantras possess greater potency (*vīryavattara*), the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* states: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*), that alone becomes more potent. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10)
"...so it is. Regarding this, it is explained as follows: "Rites are performed as revealed by mantras; there is no rite without a mantra.
[This is a censure of rites devoid of mantras.
In the *Atharvaveda*: "The ones called *ṛc*, *yajus*, and *sāman*..."
Regarding the passage from the *Āraṇyaparvan*: "The rites which the sages perceived in the mantras... and:
"By means of the vows and the initiation, or by fasting, the twice-born..."

[78.3] “And one who is joined with ritual actions and mantras would be a Brāhmaṇa; of this there is no doubt. [MBh 3.81.134] [78.4] In that very same place: “In the absence of the qualities, the fruit is deficient or indeed non-existent; but in the case of non-commencement, neither fruit nor quality is seen at all. [MBh 3.33.48]
In the *Bṛhannāradīya*: "Whatever oblation is offered to Jātavedas without mantras,
and whatever is given to an unworthy recipient— that is a terrible means of enjoyment."

Whatever oblation has been offered, whatever gift has been given by an impure person, and whatever ritual act has been performed— all that is worthy of being your portion, yielding as its fruit a fall into the lower realms.
[Br̥hannāradaP 78.10] Thus it was said by the Blessed One Vāmana to the universal monarch Bali.
[78.11] Bodhāyana: "By means of cattle, horses, vehicles, agriculture, and service to the king..."
“Families that are deficient in sacred formulas (mantra) fall from the status of a noble family;
[BaudhDhS 1.5.10.28] but families that are well-endowed with sacred formulas, even if possessing little wealth, are reckoned among the noble families and attain great renown. [BaudhDhS 1.5.10.29]
Manu also says: "Through improper marriages, the omission of sacred rites, the failure to study the Vedas, and by showing disrespect toward Brahmins, noble families fall into a state of ignobility.
[They may rise again] solely through craftsmanship, commerce, and the birth of pure offspring. (Manu Dharmashāstra 3.63)

[78.18] By means of cattle, horses, vehicles, agriculture, and service to kings; [78.19] by officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice, and by the practice of atheism—[78.20] families that are deficient in sacred mantras fall from their noble status to that of being base. (Manu Dharmashāstra 3.64–65)
“However, through the power of mantras, families that possess few riches become prosperous;
they attain the status of noble lineages and acquire great renown.
(Manu Dharmashāstra 3.66) Furthermore, it is recorded in the *Somotpatti* that “the śrāddha rite which is purified by mantras... [is most effective].
And in the Śrīgītā: “A sacrifice devoid of ritual injunctions, without the distribution of food, lacking mantras and sacrificial fees, and bereft of faith, is declared to be tāmasa.”
Thus it has been said [BhGī = MBh 6.39.13].

Furthermore, that the fruit corresponds to the mode of worship is established by scripture: "In whatever way a person intends in this world, so does he become after departing from here" [Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 14.7.2.8–10].
Therefore, because all rites accompanied by mantras are prescribed for the bodily sacraments (*saṃskāra*), there is completeness.
Precisely because of its perfection, the supremacy of this sūtra among all sūtras is established; thus has the fourth reason been explained.
[79.8] This concludes the explanation of the fourth reason. [The explanation of the fifth reason;]
[The Vaikhānasa Sūtra as the Source for Initiatory Rites such as Niṣeka] [80.1] Now follows the determination of the five reasons.
[80.2–5] Now, regarding the supreme excellence of this Śrī-Vaikhānasa Sūtra, [it concerns] those who perform the duties prescribed in that Sūtra...

Furthermore, in order to indicate that while the possession of purificatory rites such as *niṣeka* and so forth— which is logically untenable as a primary attribute for other sūtras even if they were considered supreme— is indeed logically tenable as a primary attribute for this sūtra alone, the fifth reason, "because of the possession of purificatory rites such as *niṣeka*," is set forth as follows:
[The primacy of the *niṣeka* among the *saṃskāras*]:
“[Now we shall explain the *saṃskāras*, beginning with the *niṣeka*; having begun thus with the words “at the time of union during the fertile period,” [the text continues].

[80.7] By the end of the passage beginning with “the taking of the hand,” the bodily consecrations (*śārīrasaṃskāra*) are presented as being preceded by the consecration of impregnation (*niṣekasaṃskāra*).
[Without impregnation, the birth of offspring is impossible.
[80.8–11] Now, one might ask: how can the impregnation, which occurs after birth (*jāta*), the initiation (*upanayana*), and marriage (*vivāha*), be established as the beginning?

Likewise, since birth without the *niṣeka* (conception rite) is observed in such Vedic and Smṛti passages as "The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth" and "Then Dakṣa created beings by means of the mind alone," for what purpose is the *niṣeka* established as the beginning?
Furthermore, the status of the *jātaka* (birth rite) as the beginning is understood from the *Śrībhārata*.
“Purified by those sacramental rites beginning with the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*), he is pure;
perfected in the study of the Vedas, he is established in the six duties. Devoted to purity and right conduct, seeking alms appropriately, and dear to his teacher.”
[80.15] “One who is constant in his vows and devoted to truth—he indeed is called a *brāhmaṇa*. [MBh 12.182.3] [80.16] Likewise, in the *Harivaṃśa*:
“Where are wives? Where is social attachment? And where is the perversion of one’s true nature?”
“If this mental progeny was created by Brahmā through his mind,
[then] if there is the power of asceticism in you who have realized the Self,
create mental sons through the rite pertaining to Prajāpati.”

[80.20] If it is argued that since birth is heard of even without *niṣeka* (conception), it is impossible for *niṣeka* to be the beginning—[80.21–23] that is incorrect. The claim that "birth is possible even in the absence of *niṣeka*" is not tenable. For the Blessed One Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, or the great sages possess the power to create mental offspring through the force of asceticism (*tapas*) and the power of yoga (*yoga*).
This is possible for them, but not for others. As it says in the Śrī Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"From the mere intention, from seeing, and from touching, offspring were produced by those of old. (ViṣṇuP)
“Of those supreme ascetics who are inflamed by the special power of their austerities...
[ViṣṇuP 1.15.79] “In every age these best of sages, Dakṣa and the others, come into being; and again they are dissolved. The wise man is not deluded in this regard. [ViṣṇuP 1.15.83]

“O best of the twice-born, among these there was previously neither the state of being the youngest nor the state of being the eldest; austerity alone was weightier, and spiritual power was the sole cause. [Viṣṇu Purāṇa] [Thus, even Rudra’s birth occurred through *niṣeka* alone.]
[81.7] It is also heard that the birth of Rudra occurs through the *niṣeka* (conception). In the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*:

beginning with “Indeed, this entire world was established,” [it continues] up to “And Prajāpati consecrated himself for the year of the beings; he was the lord of the household for the beings. [81.8–10]

Having stated, "Uṣas was the wife," and so forth, it continues: "The Lord of Beings, Saṃvatsara, poured his seed into Uṣas; in the course of a year a boy was born; he performs the naming ceremony for that Rudra," and so on. [The procedure for the rite of impregnation.]

[81.11-13] Indeed, the procedure for the act of impregnation is also heard: “Having made [the woman] naked, he initiates [the act] upon her thigh; for when she is naked upon the thigh, then they couple, then the semen is emitted, and then offspring are born. And:
“From the very semen that has been emitted, he transforms it into many forms; that indeed is born, and day by day it becomes more abundant.”

“[The embryo] emits semen and urine, enters the womb with its organ, is enveloped by the placenta, and leaves the amnion at birth. Thus [it is said]. In the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*: “A man pours his seed into a woman; many offspring, similar in form, are being produced. In the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, beginning with “Woman, O Gautama, is indeed fire,” and continuing with “her lap...”
"The fuel is thus: what he does within is its flame; the delights are its sparks. Into that fire the gods offer semen; from that oblation, the embryo comes into being.
And: "[From the time of creation, birth occurs precisely from the act of impregnation]."
In the *Śrī Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"O great-minded one, hear how Dakṣa, having been previously commanded by the Self-born One to 'create progeny,' created all beings. [ViṣṇuP 1.15.86]
[81.21] At that time, Dakṣa first created beings by means of his mind alone:
[81.22] the gods, the ṛṣis, the gandharvas, the asuras, and likewise the pannagas.
[81.23] But when those creatures did not multiply even as he was creating them,
[81.24] Then, having reflected many times for the sake of creation, Prajāpati,
[82.1] desiring to bring forth various offspring through the very law of sexual union,
[82.2] from that time forward, O Maitreya, living beings were born of sexual union. [ViṣṇuP 1.15.79ab?]
In the *Bhārata*: “O bull of the Bharatas, sexual intercourse was not the practice among them;
rather, by mere intention (*saṅkalpa*), an embryo was produced in them.
In that period of the Tretā Yuga, offspring were born from physical contact.”
“For even among them, O lord of men, the practice of sexual union did not exist.
In the Dvāpara age, O king, sexual union arose among progeny;
likewise, in the time of the Kali age, people entered into couples. [MBh 12.200.36–37]

[82.9–10] Thus, since it is heard in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* that [the status of being a twice-born] begins from the time of conception (*niṣeka*) and arises precisely from that, and because there is no capacity for production without *niṣeka*, it has been stated that [one becomes a twice-born] "by possessing *niṣeka* and so forth.
[The Determination of the Meaning of the Word *Niṣeka*] [82.11–13] On this point, the followers of Āpastamba say: "What is called *niṣeka* is indeed the rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*)."

Since *niṣeka* and *garbhādhāna* are synonymous, and because no other meaning for the word *niṣeka* is possible apart from *garbhādhāna*, when the meaning of the term *garbhādhāna* is examined— according to the etymology "that in which the embryo (*garbha*) is placed" and following the Vedic text "the embryo is indeed the sense organ" (*indriyaṃ vai garbhaḥ*)— it is understood that *garbhādhāna* is simply the emission of semen (*retassecanam*). Thus, the status of being preceded by *niṣeka* belongs to us as well.
Having begun thus, [the text continues]: "Then he approaches her," with the words, "O Pūṣan, you... [82.20–23].
In this way, the *niṣeka* (conception rite) has been described. Next, we shall explain the procedure for *garbhādhāna* (the impregnation rite). During the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day...

Having served food to the Brāhmaṇas under an auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) and having caused them to pronounce the *puṇyāha* (auspicious day), one then performs the rites beginning with the preparation of the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) up to the *agnimukha* (introductory oblation to Agni), and offers the cooked oblation (*pakvāj*) with the verse: "To the wise seer (*kavi*), the purifier... Thus, the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite) has been described.
Since *niṣeka* (the act of impregnation) and *garbhādhāna* are thus mentioned as distinct, it is incorrect to say that *niṣeka* alone is the *garbhādhāna*.

[82.24-25] Furthermore, because they are not mentioned as being preceded by *niṣeka* in the *Āpastamba-sūtra*, and because they are not included in the enumeration of the forty sacraments (*saṃskāra*), these sacraments beginning with *niṣeka* do not belong to them.
[83.1-6] On this point, the followers of Āpastamba said: "If it is claimed that for us the sacraments beginning with *niṣeka* do not exist, then it is exactly the same for you;
for in your own Sūtra it is stated: 'Because of this: *dhuta*, *prahuta*, *āhuta*, *śūlagava*, *baliharaṇa*, *pratyavarohaṇa*..."

Since there is no presentation of the definition of *garbhādhāna*— which is prescribed separately by the passage beginning with "for her who has bathed on the fourth day" (*caturthyāṃ snātāyām*) etc., as well as the *aṣṭakā* and *pārvaṇahoma*— and because there is no specific determination of its time,
[the status of possessing sacraments such as *niṣeka* belongs only to the Vaikhānasas].
[83.7] Furthermore, because it is stated in the *Vaikhānasa-sūtra* itself that [the rites] begin with *niṣeka*, for the *Vaikhānasas* the sequence begins with *niṣeka*.
[83.8] "For both of us, the sacraments do not begin with *niṣeka*"—this alone is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
[Others possess sacraments beginning with *garbhadhāna*.]
And thus: "For them, the rites beginning with the impregnation and ending at the cemetery are indeed performed through mantras.
[Yājñavalkya Dharmasūtra 1.10cd] The *garbhādhāna* (conception rite) is performed during the fertile period; the *puṃsavana* (rite for a male child) is before the movement of the fetus."

Regarding this statement by Yājñavalkya [YājñavalkyaDhŚ 1.11ab], according to the principle that “when a primary sense is possible, it is improper to resort to a secondary one,” the word *teṣām* (of them) refers primarily to the Vaikhānasas, because the status of beginning with the *niṣeka* rite is already established in the Śrīvaikhānasasūtra itself. Thus, they are the Vaikhānasas.
Thus they are referred to—only for them does the status of being "beginning with *niṣeka* (conception)" apply;

for others, the status of being "beginning with *niṣeka*" is not possible, but rather only the status of being "beginning with *garbhādhāna* (impregnation). This indeed is the intention of Yājñavalkya.
Now, it might be argued: "It was stated that the definition of *garbhādhāna* was not mentioned specifically, and its timing was also not mentioned."
Regarding this, it is said in the *Śrī Vaikhānasa Sūtra*, composed by the supreme teacher Vikhanas, who is the cause of all: "Now,

having recognized the signs indicating that a woman has conceived— namely, physical heaviness, sinking of the thighs, aversion to the husband, lack of appetite for food, excessive salivation, harshness of speech, and throbbing of the vulva— one should, knowing the divine connection of the embryo, [perform the rites] during the waxing fortnight."
Since the *Vaikhānasa-sūtra* also prescribes the timing characterized by conception through such passages as, "In an auspicious month, under a constellation named Puṇya," and so forth:
"The dharma that is proclaimed in the Veda and in the Vaikhānasa-sūtra— That dharma should be practiced by all; no hesitation should be made in this matter. (83.21–22)

Since this was stated by Bhṛgu, and according to the maxim that "what is not mentioned [in one source] should be taken from another," and because Vikhanas must be established as an authority in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts, it is appropriate for us as well to perform those parts not mentioned here according to the method taught by Vaikhānasa. This alone is more reasonable. For instance:
[the non-synonymity of *niṣeka* and *garbhādhāna*].

[84.1–10] Regarding Āpastamba and others, the teacher Bodhāyana addressed his own disciples, beginning with: “Now, here follows the expiation for the *pākayajñas*,” up to: “Regarding the employment of the *vyāhṛtis*, the teachers declare that what was performed incorrectly becomes correctly performed. On this point, they also cite an example.”

“From the fourth day until the sixteenth, he approaches [his wife] on each successive later night. ‘Approaching during the fertile season (*ṛtu*) leads to the excellence of progeny,’ so say the teachers. ‘All acts of approaching are accompanied by mantras,’ says Baudhāyana. ‘Both that which is at the beginning and that which is during the season,’ says Śālīki. Now, his guests may be one who follows the same conduct as his teacher, a forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*), or a *snātaka*.

"A king who is endowed with righteousness, upon their arrival, should rise and offer them a seat, water for the feet, hospitality, or the guest-offering (arghya)"—and "The teachers say that the single Agnihotra begins in the evening and concludes in the morning; regarding this, they cite [the following]";

and "One should not bear malice toward the Vaikhānasas," and so forth—in these sūtras, it is appropriate to state that the teacher referred to by the phrase "the teachers say" is indeed the Vaikhānasa, because Manu and others do not speak of the bodily consecrations (*śārīrasaṃskāra*).
Because it exists within the *Vaikhānasasūtra* propounded by Baudhāyana,
and because Baudhāyana himself stated, “[The *vaikhānasa* is one whose conduct is equal to that of the guru],” as in the phrase “by the teacher Vikhanas.”

And because it has been established in the *Bhārata*. Furthermore, since it was composed by Vikhanas, who is the cause of all [authoritative traditions], it is indeed proper for everyone to perform [the rites] according to the method stated in that *Sūtra*. Moreover, the characteristics of the sacrificial vessels, such as the *araṇi* and so forth, are also explained in that very same work.
Others also say: "Our [tradition] is also the same regarding the sequence beginning with *niṣeka* (conception). That too is incorrect.

[84.15] When the meaning of the term *garbhādhāna* (conception) is investigated, according to the authoritative testimony: “The seed entering the womb, covered by the placenta, is the embryo (*garbha*)” [84.16–20], it is understood that only the semen having entered the cavity of the womb is denoted by the word *garbha*, and not merely the semen alone. Likewise: “May Prajāpati pour [it]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo.”

Thus, because the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*) occurs immediately after the act of impregnation (*niṣeka*), and because it is possible to perform the *niṣeka* at every menstrual period, whereas [if they were distinct] there would follow the fault of emission for one who has not restrained his semen, and because that would contradict the Śruti and Smṛti as well as direct perception, it is improper to say that the *niṣeka* itself is the *garbhādhāna*.

[The Preeminence of Those Possessing the First Sacrament of Conception] [84.21] Now, if it is asked what the distinction is regarding the starting point at conception (*niṣeka*), it is said: only for those who possess the rites beginning with conception [84.22] have *śrotriyatva* (Vedic learning), eligibility for the *dharmaśāstra*, and the status of having a "brahminical body" been declared by Bodhāyana and others. As follows:

[84.23] “At the consecration, at the rites for the embryo, and at the birth ceremonies, they were duly consecrated with mantras; having observed their vows until their completion, [84.24] they were perfected through the ritual.”
Those twice-born who have mastered the branches of their Veda are to be known as *śrotriyas*;
they are those who have duly taken the hand [in marriage] during the proper season and have fulfilled their vows.
“By means of ritual application accompanied by mantras, they caused conception in a Brāhmaṇī woman;
the sacred rites beginning with the *niṣeka* (conception) and ending with the *śmaśāna* (funeral) are dependent upon the Brāhmaṇas.
Thus says Yājñavalkya.
“The rites for them, beginning with the impregnation and ending with the cremation ground, are indeed performed with mantras.
Conception should take place during the fertile period, and the *puṃsavana* rite before the fetus moves.”
Thus [YājñavalkyaDhŚ 1.11ab];

and Manu says: "He for whom the rites beginning with the *niṣeka* (conception) and ending at the *śmaśāna* (funeral pyre) have been prescribed by means of mantras—his eligibility for this scripture should be known, and not that of anyone else" [ManuDhŚ 2.16].

In this statement of Manu, because of the consequence that words such as "of whomsoever," "of that person," and "of anyone" would be redundant, it is improper to say that "for all [castes], the status beginning with the *niṣeka* is the same.
In the *Aśvamedhika* [Parvan], the Blessed One says:
"For the twice-born, the rites beginning with the *niṣeka* are performed through meritorious Vedic rituals..."
The purifying refinement of the body should be performed, which is beneficial both in this world and after death;
it is accomplished through rites pertaining to the womb, the *jātakarman*, naming, tonsure, and initiation (*upanayana*);
through Vedic study, austerities, and the vows of marriage and the *snātaka*.
“By means of the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) and the ritual sacrifices (*yajña*), this body is made fit for Brahman. Thus it is stated in the *Mahābhārata* (14, App.
4.2516). This should be understood similarly in other places as well.
Baudhāyana, in the beginning of his *Sūtra*, states that marriage must precede [the rites], beginning with the words: “Because of this, it is offered,” and so forth.

Āpastamba begins with, "Now the rites that are grasped from conduct (*ācāra*) and so forth," and continues up to, "We shall explain the initiation (*upanayana*). Bhāradvāja and Satyāṣāḍha, as well as Āśvalāyana, begin with, "The *vaitānika* (sacrificial) rites have been stated," and proceed by making the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice the starting point. Drāhyāyaṇa says, "Now, therefore, the domestic rites (*gṛhyakarmāṇi*)."

Beginning with the phrase "the first fortnight of the northern solstice" (*udagayanapūrvapakṣa*), [the rites] are presented as being preceded by proper conduct (*ācāra*) and so forth. And Kātyāyana, beginning with "Now, therefore, the rites of the domestic cooked oblations" (*athāto gṛhyasthālīpākānāṃ karma*), has expounded them.

Furthermore, the venerable Vikhanas himself, beginning with "Now we shall explain the sacraments starting with the impregnation" (*atha niṣekādisaṃskārān vyākhyāsyāmaḥ*), has expounded them as being preceded by the *niṣeka* (impregnation).

And thus, because it has been stated that this [work] is preceded by the *niṣeka* (consecration), its status as the supreme among all sūtras is established; furthermore, it is demonstrated through the medium of the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and so forth, that the preeminence of those who follow the sūtras is achieved solely through the practice of the dharmas taught in this sūtra—
this concludes the exposition of the fifth reason.
[85.25] Thus concludes the examination of the five causes.
[Examination of the sixth cause] [The *Vaikhānasasūtra* as the expositor of the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*)].

[86.1] Now, the examination of the sixth reason: [86.2–4] Now, it is possible that for those who perform the duties prescribed in the Śrī Vaikhānasa Sūtra alone, there exists— unmentioned in other sūtras— the state of being the most excellent among all, the possession of the eighteen sacraments (saṃskāra) established by the Śruti, and an abundance of ritual acts (kriyā).

In order to demonstrate that [the Veda] prescribes eighteen sacraments (*saṃskāra*), the sixth reason is set forth: "Because it teaches the eighteen sacraments. For it is said: "[86.5–8] 'Now we shall explain the sacraments beginning with conception: union during the fertile period, impregnation, the rite for a male child, the parting of the hair, the *viṣṇubali*, the birth-rite, the rite of rising from the bed, the naming, the first feeding of solid food, the return from a journey, the rite of increasing the body, the tonsure, the initiation, the study of the Vedas, the binding of the vows, the release of the vows, the supplementary ritual, the return home, and the taking of the hand.'"

“The eighteen bodily refinements (*saṃskāra*)”—thus the eighteen refinements are set forth in the Sūtra. And these, as established by the Śruti in the investigation of the meaning of the scriptural passage [“Among those in whom the inferior rite is said to be eighteen-fold” (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.7)], are found in the Śruti. As it says in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad: “For these forms of sacrifice are but frail rafts; among them, the inferior rite is said to be eighteen-fold. Those fools who rejoice in this as the highest good...”
“They return once again to old age and death.
Regarding this, some have said:
“There are sixteen officiating priests (ṛtvij) of the sacrifice, the seventeenth is the member of the assembly (sadasya), and the eighteenth is the sacrificer (yajamāna).”

[86.12–14] Thus, following the *Śruti*, it is claimed that in the passage, "In which the eighteenfold [rite] is said to be the lowest," it is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and others who are intended. That is incorrect, because it has been stated: "In which the eighteenfold rite (*karman*) is said to be the lowest. For the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the sacrificer, and so forth, are the performers of the sacrifice (*yāga*), but they are not the rite (*karman*) itself. Furthermore, the word "in which" (*yeṣu*) means "in which sūtras."

"Inferior action" refers to the *jātaka* rites and so forth, because they are actions prescribed by the *Smṛti*. Sacrifices and the like, as well as birth-rites (*jātakarma*) and so forth, are devoid of the qualities of the self. "Unstable rafts" refers to these.

They do not become crossers of saṃsāra. Thus, in this context, the formative forces (*saṃskāras*)—such as sacrifices and the like—which are censured for being like unstable rafts, are intended precisely as being devoid of the qualities of the self (*ātman*). When conjoined with that [self], they become the means for achieving liberation. As it is said: "[Formative forces devoid of the qualities of the self are the cause of bondage]."
In the Gautama-dharma:

"He who possesses the forty sacraments but lacks the eight qualities of the self does not attain union with or residence in the same world as Brahmā. But he who possesses even a portion of the forty sacraments and the eight qualities of the self—then he [attains it]."
"He attains union with Brahman (sāyujya) and residence in the same world as Brahman (sālokya).
[The characteristics of the eight qualities of the self: "The eight qualities of the self (aṣṭāv ātmaguṇāḥ):"
“Compassion toward all beings, patience, freedom from envy, purity, lack of exertion, auspiciousness, lack of miserliness, and lack of longing. As for their characteristics:
[therein, the characteristic of compassion is:
“[86.24] ‘Whether toward a non-relative or a circle of relatives, toward a friend or an enemy, likewise...’”
But that which is the protection of one who has fallen into misfortune is proclaimed as compassion (dayā).
[In that regard, the characteristic of patience: [87.1] Whether suffering is produced by others externally or internally,
[87.2] that one does not become angry and does not strike back— that is proclaimed as patience.
[Therein, the characteristic of non-envy: One does not disparage those who possess virtues,
nor does one praise even those with meager virtues.
That which does not take delight in the faults of others is proclaimed as "freedom from envy" (anasūyā).
[In that regard, the definition of purity:
[87.5] Avoidance of forbidden food, association with those who are blameless, and steadfastness in one's own duty— this is declared to be purity.
[In that regard, the characteristic of effortlessness: [87.7] Whatever action, even if very beautiful, causes the body to suffer, that must never be performed; it is called "effortless. [87.8]
[In that regard, the characteristic of auspiciousness:
[87.9] Constantly performing what is praiseworthy and abandoning what is not praiseworthy—this indeed has been declared as auspicious by the seers who perceive reality. [87.10]
[In that regard, the characteristic of non-miserliness:
[87.11] One should give even from a small amount with an undepressed inner self; [87.12] whatever is given day after day, however little it may be, that is called non-miserliness.
[In that regard, the characteristic of non-longing:
"Just as one should practice contentment with wealth that has come to hand, one should not speak for the sake of others' interests; this is proclaimed as non-longing. Thus it is said.
[87.15] This was stated as a digression. Let us now follow the main subject.
[Regarding the *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* Purāṇas:

[87.16–17] If it is argued that the meaning of the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* is that the eighteen-fold duties mentioned in the Smṛtis are what are mentioned in the eighteen Purāṇas, that too is incorrect. For in the Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and so forth, there is the "eighteenfold duty" (*aṣṭādaśakarma*).

In this regard, since it was stated in general terms that "the eighteen are said to be the lowest form of action," it is appropriate to say that the yoga and other practices mentioned therein are not taught in the *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas*, because they lack the capacity to lead to liberation and, moreover, result in old age and death. Furthermore:
In the *Padma Purāṇa*:
“The *Vaiṣṇava*, the *Nāradīya*, and likewise the auspicious *Bhāgavata*;
the *Gāruḍa*, the *Pādma*, and the *Vārāha*, O lady of auspicious appearance.”
[Padma Purāṇa, Uttarabhāga 236.19] [The Preeminence of Sāttvika Purāṇas] [88.1] Six distinct Purāṇas should be known as sāttvika.
The Brahmāṇḍa, the Brahmakaivarta, and likewise the Mārkaṇḍeya;
The future Vāmana Purāṇa and the Brāhma Purāṇa are of the nature of *rajas*, and there are six such types.
Know from me that these six— the Mātsya, Kaurma, Laiṅga, Śaiva, Skānda, and Āgneya— are characterized by tamas.
Thus it is said in the *Padma Purāṇa* (Uttarabhāga 236.18):

"Mixed, tamasic, rajasic, and likewise sattvic—these four kinds of kalpas are declared to be the days of Brahmā. And in the *Mātsya Purāṇa*: "Mixed, tamasic, rajasic, and likewise sattvic—these four kinds of kalpas are declared to be the days of Brahmā. (88.6–7)
In whichever eon a Purāṇa was proclaimed by Brahmā in the past,
its greatness exists in that very form;
it is recounted among the mixed [traditions] of Sarasvatī and the Pitṛs.
[88.11] The majesty of Agni and Śiva is proclaimed in the *tāmasa* [ages];
[88.12] but in the *rājasa* [ages], they know the majesty of Brahmā to be greater;
[88.13] and in the *sāttvika* kalpas, the majesty of Hari is supreme.
“Only those who have attained perfection in yoga shall go to the supreme goal,” so it is said in the *Matsya Purāṇa*.
In the *Padma Purāṇa*: “The *Vāsiṣṭha*, the *Hārīta*, the *Vyāsa*, and likewise the *Pārāśara*...”
The Bhāradvāja, the Kāśyapīya, the Smṛtiṣaṭka, the Sāttvika, the Mānava, the Yājñavalkya, the Ātreya, and the Dākṣya.
The *Kātyāyana*, the *Vaiṣṇava*, and the six codes of law (*smṛti*) are of the nature of *rājasa*;
likewise, the *Gautama*, the *Bārhaspatya*, the *Sāṃvarta*, and the *Yama-smṛti*.
The Śāmbha and the Auśanasa— these six Smṛtis are characterized by tamas.
Thus [PadmaP Uttarabhāga 236.26ab] [88.21].
Likewise: "Those characterized by *sattva* are to be known as bestowing liberation; those characterized by *rajas* are remembered as bestowing heaven" [PadmaP Uttarabhāga 236.21cd].
In the same way, O Goddess, those characterized by darkness (tāmasa) are the causes for falling into hell.

Because it is remembered that the worship of the Lord and other such practices, established in the Sāttvika Purāṇas through statements such as [PadmaP Uttarabhāga 236.22ab] [88.23–24], are causes for liberation,
it is not possible to claim that the actions described generally in the eighteen Purāṇas are like a worn-out boat.
[The abundance of rites in the Vaikhānasa tradition] [89.1–2]:

Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of accepting that heaven, liberation, and hell are of a single nature. Therefore, it should be understood that there are precisely the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) mentioned in the venerable *Vaikhānasa-sūtra*. In the *Bodhāyana-sūtra*, however, no enumeration of the purificatory rites has been made.

[89.3-5] Since Āpastamba and others accept the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) and the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*) as *pākayajñas*, and since these sixteen sacraments (*saṃskāra*) are not explicitly distinguished [by them], nor is there any presentation of other sacraments, they cannot be accepted as being stated therein.
[89.6-8] In the *Śrīvaikhānasa*, however, there is also an abundance of ritual acts. For instance: "The eighteen sacraments are *pākayajñas*..."

And they are established as distinct. However, the specific variations, such as the birthday celebrations (*varṣavardhana*) and so forth, consist of twenty-two sacrifices together with the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*);

that is, the five great sacrifices constitute one [category], and there is another category consisting of eighteen [sacrifices] in addition to those. If it is asked, "What is the significance of this abundance of ritual acts?"—it is said: in the *Muṇḍopaniṣad*:

“It is one who performs ritual action who is the best among the knowers of Brahman,” and it is also heard in scripture: “The learned ones who perform rituals, who are firmly established in Brahman, themselves offering oblations with faith to the Single Seer—to them alone should he declare this knowledge of Brahman. Thus says Bodhāyana.

"Therefore, whoever is a performer of action whose conduct is approved by the virtuous, he alone is to be known as a *śrotriya*; he alone is to be known. Furthermore, from the abundance of ritual action, the abundance of the fruit is established according to the principle that "the fruit corresponds to the mode of meditation. Therefore:
The sixth reason has been established: that this Sūtra’s excellence and its status as the most supreme among all Sūtras are justified by its teaching of the eighteen refinements (*aṣṭādaśasaṃskāra*).
[89.16] Thus concludes the exposition of the sixth reason. [Exposition of the seventh reason]

[90.1–3] Now, the seventh reason is set forth to demonstrate that the *Śrīvaikhānasasūtra* possesses independence because it contains the entire collection of ritual acts along with their constituent parts, and thus has no dependence on other *sūtras*.
For instance, in this *sūtra*, the eighteen bodily sacraments (*saṃskāras*) are presented exactly as they are well-known, together with their constituent parts.

[90.4–8] If it is objected: "But surely, since there is no instruction on the planting of seedlings (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), the hundredfold consecration (*śatābhiṣeka*), the two-fold fire-union (*agnidvayasaṃsarga*), the adoption of a son (*putraparigraha*), the *brahmamedha*, the *vṛṣotsarga*, and so forth, this work does not possess the full range of ritual procedures (*sāṅgakriyākalāpavattva*)," that is incorrect. This doubt arises from a lack of familiarity with the nature of the *Śrīvaikhānasasūtra*.
This *Sūtra* consists of eleven sections (*praśna*). To say that these [rites] are not expounded herein—

This is because they are perceived as being supplementary, due to the lack of knowledge regarding the existence of the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*. If it is asked how the existence of the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa* is understood, it is said in reply:
beginning with the words, "Now we shall explain the ritual for the offering of sprouts" (*athāṅkurārpaṇavidhiṃ vyākhyāsyāmaḥ*), the offering of sprouts is described in two sections.

Furthermore, in the passage, "In the evening, one fashions a thousand forms of Soma out of flour upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*)," there is a specific presentation of the sacrificial mound and other details.
[90.12] “In the forenoon, the hundredfold consecration, the auspicious day, and the feeding of the twice-born.”
Beginning with these words, [Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa 90.13–14]:
“In the evening, on a leveled ground smeared with cow-dung that is elevated toward the east,
one should draw there fifty-two lines facing the east.”
And likewise, one should draw thirty-two lines toward the north.
By the passage beginning with “[Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa S] 90.16,” the procedure for the hundredfold consecration (*śatābhiṣeka*) has been stated.
Likewise, starting from “[Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa S] 90.17”: “The two [the bride and groom] should wear washed garments,” and so forth.
[90.18] “In a house adorned with lamps and other ornaments, having indeed spread grains of rice there, [90.19] in the absence of a skin, one may use a mat; above that, one should spread a cloth.”

Thus [Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa 90.20]: "At the concluding oblation, at the end of the internal oblations, while both are seated there upon the skin, he should cast off that skin with the words: 'I release the vow. [90.21] He should abandon that skin with the mantra: "I release the vow."
By the passage beginning with [Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa 90.22], the method for the conjunction of two fires has been set forth; [at 91.1],
the method for the formal adoption of a son is also explained.
[91.2] Even though renunciation, sale, and giving have been mentioned therein, according to the Smṛti:
[91.3] "One should not give away a single [item], nor should a woman accept one without her husband's permission."

By such passages as these, the procedure for the *brahmamedha* (the sacrifice unto Brahman) is described [Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa 91.4]: "This is the sacrament for those who are established in Brahman and who possess virtuous conduct. [91.5]
The Brahmamedha sacrifice yields abundant fruit, yet it is not for all members of the twice-born.
By such passages as these, the ritual for the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) is described [in Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa 91.7–8]:
“I shall declare the ritual for the release of a bull, by which liberation from the state of a *preta* is attained.”
Then, having bathed at the conclusion of the Vāstu-homa, for the sake of liberation from the state of being a preta, [one should perform the following].
By such statements as these [Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa 91.10], it should be understood that all matters not mentioned here have been declared in the Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa [91.11–15].

If it is argued that Bodhāyana and others have also presented these [rites] together with their ancillaries (*sāṅga*), we say no; for [the maxim applies]: "When the wall exists... [the painting follows].

If the primary rites have been expounded according to the principle of "the subsidiary [is understood] from the principal," then an investigation of the subsidiaries must be undertaken. Regarding the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), the offering of the *arghya* water and so forth has not been mentioned.

Furthermore, the undertaking of the forest-dweller stage of life (*vānaprasthāśrama*) and other such matters have not been set forth. There is indeed a dependence upon the *Vaikhānasa-sūtra* regarding the undertaking or non-undertaking of the forest-dweller stage, the gathering of forest produce, the characteristics of ritual vessels, and so on. While the installation of deities and the like have been mentioned, their specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) have not been stated.

Āpastamba and others have not mentioned even such matters as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), the ritual germinating of seeds (*aṅkura*), the propitiation of deities for the *pratisara* thread, or the wearing of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). It is well known that Āpastamba and the others depend upon one another; this mutual dependence is a lack of independence, like being deficient in a limb.
Manu says: "Whatever action depends on another, that one should avoid with effort" (MDhŚ 4.159cd).
[91.20] “Everything dependent on another is suffering; everything dependent on oneself is happiness.
[91.21] One should know this, in brief, to be the defining characteristic of happiness and suffering.

[Manu Dharmashāstra 4.160] [91.22–23] By this, the attainment of infinite and stable fruit is shown. Therefore, because it is independent of other sūtras, its status as the supreme among all sūtras and its autonomy are established; thus, the seventh [chapter] has been analyzed.
[91.24] Thus concludes the examination of the seventh cause. [Now begins the examination of the eighth cause: the fact that the Vaikhānasa-sūtra is accepted by all learned authorities.]

“Abiding by the doctrine of the Vaikhānasas, he should always subsist solely on flowers, roots, and fruits that have ripened in due time and fallen of their own accord.”

Hārīta: A forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) should avoid cultivated plants. Having established the *śrāmaṇaka* fire in place of the three sacred fires (*tretāgni*), and wearing garments made of bark, hemp, skin, *kuśa* grass, *muñja* grass, or split bamboo, he becomes a *vaikhānasa* according to the rule proclaimed by Vikhanas. He is both one who has received permission (*anujñāyika*) and one who follows the path of the forest (*anuprasthāyika*).

[Vasiṣṭha: "Having established the *śrāmaṇaka* fire, he becomes one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) while dwelling at the foot of trees. [Vasiṣṭha Dharmasūtra 9.10] [Baudhāyana: "The forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) follows the practice prescribed in the *Vaikhānasa* scriptures.
