The domestic fire (*aupāsana*) is established on account of the marriage ceremony.

In the *Jaiminīya-sūtra*, within the section on the *Saumika-cāturmāsya* sacrifices, it is stated: "As previously [described] by Bhāradvāja, so [is it] previously by Vaikhānasa; thus [it is] fivefold.
[This indicates that the acceptance of all learned authorities (*akhila-śiṣṭa*) is the cause for the excellence of its authority.]

[93.1–2] Regarding both of these, the commentary states: "From among the sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), one should choose as the *prastotṛ* a follower of the Bhāradvāja-sūtra, and as the *pratihartr̥* a follower of the Vaikhānasa-sūtra.
[93.3] In the Kapiñjala-saṃhitā:
[93.4] "One who is engaged in officiating at sacrifices and teaching, and who bestows favor upon his disciples..."

One who is devoted to the mantras and tantras should be known as an *ācārya*. Whether in a hermitage or in the forest, one who is settled with his son and wife and is constantly intent upon the eight-syllable mantra is called a *vaikhānasa*.
One who dwells in the forest should avoid all vulgar practices;
clothed in bark and deerskin, he is called a silent sage (maunī).
Thus, in the *Pādmapurāṇa*, in the section on the twelve-syllable mantra,
[it is said]: "...endowed with wife and children."
Whether in a forest or even in a city, the pure hermit should recite [the mantra].
“Separated from wife, children, and the like, he dwells alone in the forest. [Padma Purāṇa] (93.14) Others have also stated exactly this.

(93.15–16) If it is asked, “What is the distinction in being accepted by all the learned?”—it is understood that there is a superior degree of authoritative validity (*prāmāṇya*) due to its acceptance by all the learned.
In the *Āśvamedhika*:
“For those desiring to know the Dharma, the first authority is the Śruti;
the second is indeed the Dharmaśāstra, and the third is the consensus of the world. Thus it is said. (MBh 14, App. 4.2492–2493)

[93.19] Manu says: “Learn that Dharma which is correctly practiced by the wise who are forever free from hatred and passion, and which is approved by the heart. [Manu Dharmashāstra 2.1] Yājñavalkya says:

“A council of four who know the Vedic dharma, or even one of those who have mastered the three Vedas, declares: ‘This is the Dharma,’ provided that he alone is the most excellent among those who know the inner self.”
The Vedas are authoritative; the Smṛtis are authoritative; and speech endowed with righteousness and purpose is authoritative.
For one for whom authority does not exist as authority—who could make his word authoritative?
He for whom neither the Vedas nor the treatises on Dharma,
nor the words of the elders, constitute authority— he is a doer of unrighteousness, struck down by evil, and wicked-souled.
Even its own self would be the means of valid cognition for that very thing.
[On the threefold justification for the Vedic basis of Smṛti:

Regarding the fact that Smṛti is also rooted in the Veda, a threefold justification has been provided. The Prābhākaras maintain that its root is a Vedic revelation (śruti) that is eternally inferable.

"Among them, the lost recensions (*utsanna-pāṭha*) are inferred from their usage"—thus [state] Āpastamba and others regarding the fact that [the Smṛtis] are rooted in lost Vedic branches (*utsanna-śākhā*). This has been refuted by the Prābhākara school and others, and is not accepted by the author of the *Bhāṣya*. Even in the Prābhākara position, if it is held that they are rooted in eternally inferable revelation (*nityānumeya-śruti*), this must be either in terms of the individual syllables or as qualified by a specific sequence. If it is said to be "in terms of the individual syllables," then [this would apply even to] words such as *ka*, *ṭa*, *pa*, and *ya*.

Furthermore, it might be argued that these [Smṛtis] possess the status of Smṛti because they are rooted in a Vedic revelation (śruti) that is eternally inferable. If it is argued that this is so "by virtue of being distinguished by a specific sequence," then their status as being eternally inferable would be lost. Regarding the position that they are rooted in lost Vedic branches (utsanna-śākhā), there are two possibilities: either those [passages] have been lost here and there within various branches, or one entire branch has been lost. If you say "here and there," that is not the case.

Because it is being studied in the form of *padapāṭha*, *kramapāṭha*, and so forth, it is not possible for it to have its source in a lost recensional branch (*utsanna-śākhā*). If it is argued that only one such branch is lost—no;

for it is impossible that Vyāsa, who was an incarnation of a portion of Viṣṇu, endowed with the power of austerity and yoga, and possessed of direct perception of all the Vedas, would remain ignorant of any [branch].
Furthermore, since it is possible for even a single disciple to have the capacity to teach it, it is untenable to speak in such a manner.
Because it is illogical. Therefore, it must be stated that the Smṛtis have their roots in the various scattered Vedic branches (śākhās). Thus it has been said:

“Vedic words are difficult to understand, especially those that are scattered and constitute the *khilas*; by those who know them, these very words—whose meanings are otherwise obscure—are established as having sixfold significance within the system of the Smṛtis.”

Therefore, because the Śrī Vaikhānasa Sūtra—which is recognized as authoritative by the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and other sources—is accepted by all learned persons (śiṣṭas), it possesses a preeminent authority; thus, the eighth reason, "because it has been adopted by Manu and others," has been established.
This concludes the exposition of the eighth reason.
[The Investigation of the Ninth Reason] [The Exclusive Devotion to Nārāyaṇa of the Followers of the Vaikhānasa Sūtras] [95.1–3] Now,

in order to demonstrate that for those who adhere to other sūtras such as those of Āpastamba, there is no unbroken lineage of exclusive devotion starting from the author of the sūtra itself, [the author addresses] the followers of the Vaikhānasa Sūtras...
In order to demonstrate that this is indeed possible, [it is said]:
“Perception, inference, and scripture consisting of various traditions—these three should be well understood by one who desires the establishment of the Dharma. (Manu Dharmashastra 12.105)

Thus, following the recollection of Manu and in order to demonstrate through perception and other means that [the Upanishads] have Śrīman Nārāyaṇa— the sole cause of the entire world— as their only supreme object, the ninth reason is set forth.
Regarding this Sūtra’s having Nārāyaṇa alone as its sole supreme object,
[there are six kinds of marks of purport].
“Commencement and conclusion, repetition, novelty, fruit, explanatory praise, and logical justification— these are the marks for determining the intended meaning.
[The fact that Nārāyaṇa alone is denoted by the term *parabrahman*]

Thus, the sixfold marks of the intended meaning (*tātparyaliṅga*) have been stated. For instance, in the first section of the initial inquiry, it is said: "devoted to Nārāyaṇa. Likewise: "One who is always delighted in the inner self (*adhyātma*), a practitioner of meditation (*dhyānayogin*), seeing the supreme Brahman which is Nārāyaṇa, should maintain concentration; he attains the imperishable supreme Brahman—'Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman,' so says the Śruti."

Thus it has been set forth in the concluding section on the rules for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). In the rites beginning with the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*) and ending with the *puṇyāha* rite, the *āghāra* oblation, the *nāndīmukha*, the initiation (*upanayana*), the marriage (*pāṇigrahaṇa*), and the funeral rites (*antakarma*), the Vaiṣṇava mantras beginning with "ato devā" are prescribed for application. Likewise, in the section on the *āghāra* oblation, the placing of the fuel (*idhmādhāna*) is performed according to the sūtra: "One should offer the reed (*śara*) into the glowing embers of the fire."
In accordance with the statement of the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa*, this is ordained in the fire of the Supreme Brahman.
[The participation of Brahmā, Rudra, and others in portions of the sacrifice is obtained through the grace of the Lord.
[95.18–96.5] Furthermore, it is determined in the Vedāntas that the Lord Nārāyaṇa alone is designated by the term "Supreme Brahman. For instance:

The state of being the cause of the world and the denotability by the word *brahman* belong to that non-different efficient and material cause— established by such passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second"— which is described by [the text] "That from which these beings are born... that is Brahman," and so forth.
It is established [as follows]. Its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is defined by purificatory statements (*śodhakavākya*), such as: "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite.
Of that [Brahman] characterized by truth and so forth, its nature as unsurpassed bliss is set forth by the statement: "Bliss is Brahman.
Such a reality, which is the form of Brahman, is [declared to be] "Nārāyaṇa, the supreme Brahman" and "That Reality is Nārāyaṇa."

By such scriptural passages as, "In the beginning, indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed," and "The divine, singular god Nārāyaṇa, free from all evil," it is determined that [the subject] is none other than the glorious Nārāyaṇa. Consequently, the word *brahman* found in the supplementary portion of the Taittirīya text, "they meditate upon [it]," refers exclusively to Nārāyaṇa;
thus, the kindling of fuel mentioned in the present sūtra also refers exclusively to Nārāyaṇa.

Likewise, in the case of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration): "Meditating upon Nārāyaṇa, having fasted"; in the *agnihotra*: "One should meditate upon Viṣṇu, the Abundant One"; in the *darśapūrṇamāsa*: "When the sun has risen, meditating upon Nārāyaṇa [while reciting] 'viṣṇor nu kam'."

Having recited thus, and because it is stated everywhere with repetition that he is devoted to Nārāyaṇa—as in the *Some*: "But one who is intent upon Nārāyaṇa remains silent"—this Sūtra refers exclusively to Nārāyaṇa.
[96.10-14] Now, an objection: in this Sūtra, regarding returning from a journey and in the month of Āśvayuja, it says: "circumambulation, worship, and prostration..."

If it is asked: "Since it is stated regarding Guha, 'Having invoked the Lord (devam),' how can it be asserted that he [Guha] is everywhere subordinate to Nārāyaṇa?"—it is replied: From the statement, "The other deities are the limbs," it is understood from the *Mahābhārata* and other sources that even those who are limbs, such as Brahmā and Rudra, receive their share of the sacrifice through the grace of the Blessed Lord; for instance: [Text follows...]

[96.15] "Then all those gods, Brahmā, and those great seers [96.16] commenced a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice according to the rite prescribed in the Vedas. [96.17] At that sacrificial session, Brahmā himself likewise assigned a portion for himself."
[96.18] The gods and the great seers all assigned their respective portions.
[96.19] Those portions, characterized by the dharma of the Kṛta age and most highly refined, [96.20] reached that Person, who is the color of the sun and beyond darkness. [MBh 12.327.50]
The Blessed One said:
"Whatever portion was conceived by whom has arrived accordingly;
being pleased, I shall today bestow upon him a fruit characterized by rebirth."
[96.23] And in all the worlds, the gods will indeed perform sacrifices in the sacrificial rites;
[96.24] those men will assign to you portions ordained by the Vedas.
[The eligibility for worship of Rudra and others as limbs of Nārāyaṇa.]
“Whoever has assigned a share to me in this great sacrifice according to his own conception, by me he has been made worthy of a share in the great sacrifice through the Vedic sūtras.
Thus [MBh 12.327.55]. In the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata:

“I am Bhava, as are Dakṣa, Bhṛgu, and the foremost others; the lords of creatures, the lord of beings, and the chief lords of the gods—all of us have entered into his discipline and bear the yoke of the world placed upon our heads.
Thus, since even Bhava and the others are understood to be worthy of worship as limbs of Nārāyaṇa.
“Worship of the gods as auxiliary members is not prohibited;
for if a Brahmin performs it with the notion that they are independent [deities], he shall go to hell.”

"Any Brahmin who worships Brahmā, Indra, or Agni without [first worshipping] Hari would certainly become a heretic. Because of such passages, and because it is recorded that there is no fault for one who performs their worship as subordinate members [of the ritual], the Sūtra speaks in that manner.
Likewise: "If worship is prescribed by superimposing something else upon you, that practice is said to have fallen away from you, as is the case with reality itself.
But if worship is prescribed by superimposing everything upon you..."
“That entire mode of conduct is to be known as yours, for your very reality is indeed yours alone.

[KJK 97.14–15] Thus, because Kaśyapa has demonstrated the distinctions in the nature of worship in the *Jñānakāṇḍa*, and because it is established by the primary aphorism that “the perpetual worship of Viṣṇu is the worship of all the gods,” and because it does not yield the fruit of falling away from one's state;

Furthermore, it is not appropriate to regard them as being for the purpose of worshiping Him (Nārāyaṇa) as His limbs. Since the *Sūtras* of Āpastamba and others establish that all purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) function through an intermediary door, and because there is not even a single instance of recollection directed solely toward Nārāyaṇa, those [texts] do not have Nārāyaṇa as their sole object of devotion.
[The absence of the status of having Nārāyaṇa as the sole object of devotion in the *Sūtras* of Āpastamba and others.]

[97.19–21] But surely Bodhāyana also, beginning with “Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual for the installation of Viṣṇu; on the twelfth, the eleventh, or the Śroṇā [constellation], or whatever other auspicious lunar mansions there may be,” and then stating the oblations and so forth with “With the twelve names: svāhā to such-and-such, svāhā to such-and-such,” and so on, has already taught this.
“We worship you alone, the primordial, ancient Person, Nārāyaṇa, the creator of the universe;
you alone are the sacrifice ordained and to be performed.”
[97.25] “O Self, accept the oblation by yourself. [BaudhGṛŚeṣS 2.13.36] [Regarding Āpastamba and others being devoted to various deities:
[98.1–5] Since it is established that they are solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa, how can it be said that their devotion to Nārāyaṇa alone does not exist?

If it is argued thus—it is true. This teacher Bodhāyana did not mention the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) and so forth with exclusive devotion to Nārāyaṇa for Āpastamba and others. However, having introduced [the topic] with: "Now we shall explain the procedure for the installation of Rudra; on the fourth, the eighth, under the asterism Ārdrā, or Apabharaṇī, or whatever other auspicious asterisms there may be," he says: "To Bhava..."
Having described the oblations and other rites with the formulas beginning with "To the god, svāhā! and "To the wife of the god Bhava, svāhā! [BaudhGṛŚeṣS 2.16.1–2], [98.6] he recites:
"Thee, the one, the primordial, ancient Puruṣa..."
“We worship Rudra, Śiva, the creator of the universe. You alone are the sacrifice ordained and to be performed; O Self, accept the oblation from the self. [BaudhGṛŚeṣS 2.16.39]
Thus ends the installation of Śiva;
likewise, beginning with the words, "Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the daily service of Mahādeva" [98.11–15],
up to "one should invoke Mahādeva— 'May the Blessed Mahādeva come,'" these are treated as distinct.

And the worship of Rudra has been established. Likewise, elsewhere, beginning with the words, "Now, therefore, on the eighth day of every half-month, the Brahmins and women say," and continuing with, "Then, at dusk, [one should invoke] Rudra Virūpākṣa, together with his wife, his sons, and his retinue," the invocation of Rudra is described. Similarly: "The Sun, Ambikā, Viṣṇu, Gaṇanātha, and Maheśvara."
Thus ends the five-fold worship (*pañcapūjā*). Therefore, the *Bodhāyana-sūtra* is not devoted exclusively to Nārāyaṇa.
Now, regarding Āpastamba and others: are they devoted exclusively to Nārāyaṇa, or rather to Rudra, or perhaps to various deities?
If it is argued that they are devoted exclusively to Nārāyaṇa, this is not so; for in matters such as caste, family, and custom, beginning from the very first of one’s own lineage (*gotra*):
[98.19] His mother-in-law observes the vow of the naked ones (Digambara); his relatives are followers of the Sugata (Buddhists).
[98.20] Both his mother and father are Pāśupatas; his teacher is a Vaiśeṣika.
[98.21] His brother abides in the systems of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and his friend is a disciple of the Cārvākas.
[98.22] “This Vedic [teacher], named Mithyācāra, is himself a subverter.

[98.23–99.4] According to this stated manner, since these practitioners of the Śaiva, Pāśupata, Vaiṣṇava, and other systems exist, the *sūtras* of Āpastamba and others are not exclusively devoted to Nārāyaṇa alone; for they lack any exposition of the rules for the propitiation of the Lord Nārāyaṇa.

Furthermore, if the *sūtras* of Āpastamba and others were solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa, then all those who practice the duties (*dharma*) prescribed in those *sūtras* would necessarily be solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa. Yet such is not observed to be the case. Regarding the attainment of Vaiṣṇava status through the path taught in the *Pāñcarātra* and other systems, [the following verses apply]: "But while one's own *sūtra* exists," "By abandoning one's own *sūtra*," and "He who abandons his own duty (*svadharma*)."

[Otherwise,] defects such as being a "heretic" (*śākhāraṇḍa*)—defined by the abandonment of one's own *sūtra* and the adoption of another's dharma as established in such statements as "One's own dharma, even if deficient, is better than the dharma of another"—would follow.

Furthermore, their conviction in the authority of their own *sūtra*, expressed in the words, "When the determination of one's own scripture is true, the determinations of the world become true," would be unavoidable.
[The Vaikhānasas' uninterrupted devotion to Nārāyaṇa.]

[99.7–9] Among the Vaikhānasas, beginning from their own Sūtrakāra, the fact that their worship and other practices are directed exclusively toward the glorious Nārāyaṇa in an uninterrupted lineage is established by direct perception. And thus says the Sūtra: “Whether in the home or in a temple, one should worship the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa with devotion; it is known that he goes to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. [99.10–12] As for the others—Āpastamba and the rest—who are related as fathers, grandfathers, maternal uncles, maternal grandfathers, sons, grandsons, brothers, or kinsmen, some are Śaivas, some are Pāśupatas, and some are Śāktas.
It is seen in such a form as being devoted to various deities.
[99.13] “Through austerity, knowledge, and meditative concentration over thousands of other births, devotion to Kṛṣṇa arises in those men whose sins have been exhausted. [99.14]

Thus, although for some it may be possible that Nārāyaṇa is supreme due to the excellence of their own previously performed merit, it cannot be said that this [supremacy] exists as an unbroken lineage starting from the author of their own Sūtras down to themselves. Therefore:
“Those whose knowledge is struck down by various desires, who worship various deities...”
[99.18] "O Blessed One, in the Kali age, men will not abide in absolute certainty.
[99.19–20] Having examined it thoroughly with their intellect through scripture, inference, direct perception, and logical reasoning, the wise person should place their faith in it. [VāyuP]

[99.21–22] Thus, having carefully examined the matter through the scriptures and other means according to the statements in the *Vāyu Purāṇa* and elsewhere, the meaning as thus determined must be practiced by the wise.
[The Supremacy of Nārāyaṇa] [99.23–100.10] Now, if it is asked: "For what purpose was the Sūtra composed with exclusive focus on Nārāyaṇa alone?"—it is replied:

Because Nārāyaṇa is the sole cause of the entire universe, because he is denoted by such terms as "Supreme Brahman" and "Supreme Self," because he bestows fruits such as liberation, and because he is without equal or superior, this work has been composed with exclusive devotion to Nārāyaṇa alone. In this regard: "From Nārāyaṇa Rudra is born; from Nārāyaṇa Indra is born; from Nārāyaṇa the twelve Ādityas, the Rudras, the Vasus, and all beings [are born]."

"From Nārāyaṇa alone they arise; into Nārāyaṇa they are dissolved"—such passages as these; beginning with "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman," up to "Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all that is within and without"—such passages as these;
and "Only by knowing him does one become immortal here; there is no other path for the journey," and "He is the Lord of immortality"—such passages as these.

“Neither his activity nor his instrument is perceived”; “Neither his equal nor his superior is seen”; “His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, as well as his innate knowledge, strength, and action”;
“This divine, singular god Nārāyaṇa is the inner self of all beings”—such passages as these, and “In the beginning, indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed,” and so forth.

“The source from which these beings are born, that by which, once born, they live, and that into which they enter when they depart—desire to know That; That is Brahman. And such scriptural passages as “the Lord of the universe, the Self-Sovereign” [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.16] are the authoritative evidence [that the Śvetāśvatara and other texts do not have the supremacy of Rudra as their primary purport].

[100.11-23] But surely—in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad—it is said: “For there is only one Rudra; he does not stand for a second. He who rules these worlds by his ruling powers, Rudra, the great seer, who is superior to all—He who in the beginning generated Hiraṇyagarbha, may He endow us with auspicious understanding. And: “The supreme Maheśvara, accompanied by Umā, the three-eyed, the blue-throated...”

If it is argued that the causality of the world and other attributes are established for Rudra as well by such passages as, "Having known that which is utterly tranquil, the Sage goes to the source of beings, the witness of all, beyond darkness," we reply: although these may appear at first glance to have Rudra as their subject, upon investigation they have Nārāyaṇa alone as their subject. The statement "Rudra is one only" is untenable, given [the scriptural mention of] "thousands upon thousands."

Since the existence of multiple Rudras is understood from Vedic passages such as "Those Rudras... and "The eleven Rudras...", it is impossible for that which is denoted by the word *rudra*—being cruel—to be denoted by the word *brahman*, given the definition: "It is proclaimed as *brahman* because of its vastness (*bṛhattva*) and its expanding nature (*bṛṃhaṇatva*)."
“Those Asuras had three cities,” beginning thus, [the text continues]:
“‘He will shoot this,’ they said to Rudra; ‘Rudra is indeed cruel, let him shoot. He said, ‘Let me choose a boon:
let me alone be the lord of cattle. Therefore Rudra is the lord of cattle. “Or rather, Rudra...”
He desired, "May I be possessed of cattle," [saying], "The mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus. This is because he was a petitioner for the status of Lord of Cattle (*paśupati*).
"Neither god nor mortal; neither the sovereign King Varuṇa, nor Agni, nor Indra, nor Pavamāna.
[This indicates the absence of equality with Nārāyaṇa on the part of Brahmā, Rudra, and the others.]

And because it is stated, beginning with "The mother is not found," up to: "This is the bow of Rudra. By means of the bow-tip belonging to Rudra, he crushed his head. That became the *pravargya*. Therefore, he who sacrifices with a sacrifice accompanied by the *pravargya* replaces the head of Rudra; Rudra does not seize him. [100.24–101.7]

It is not possible for Rudra to be denoted by the word "Brahman. It is not possible for the unity of those who are heard in scripture as being one—namely Rudra, Hara, Paśupati, Nīlagrīva, Śitikaṇṭha, Bhava, Śarva, and Kapardin—to be established, because of the hearing of the term "Paramamaheśvara" in the sequence: "Īśvara, Maheśvara, Paramamaheśvara. [As it is said: "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon; Śiva is the benefactor."

Because, through such statements as "having abandoned everything else," there exists that which is denoted by the terms *śivatara* and *śivatama* as being superior to that denoted by the term *śiva*; because the word *śambhu* is heard [in scripture] as the "one who brings peace to the universe" (*viśvaśambhu*); because Īśāna is heard as the "Lord of the world" (*jagadīśāna*);
and because of Mahādeva, [as stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad]: "Him, the supreme Maheśvara among lords, Him, the supreme deity among deities."
Furthermore, it is not possible for Rudra and others to be denoted by the term "Supreme Brahman" based on scriptural revelation (*śravaṇa*).

[Objection: But surely, since Rudra is possible as the one denoted by the term "Supreme Maheśvara" who is qualified by being accompanied by Umā in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*, it is possible for him to be denoted by the term "Supreme Brahman. [Reply: No. The term "Supreme Maheśvara" [refers to] the one accompanied by Umā...

In this context, because [the attributes] are inappropriate for Rudra and the others; the syllable *u*, however, serves the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). The meaning is: having meditated upon Lakṣmī-Narasiṃha—who is the supreme Maheśvara accompanied by Umā (Lakṣmī), and who is distinguished by specific attributes such as being three-eyed.
Alternatively, it is because he is the supreme Maheśvara in comparison to gods, humans, and so forth.
“The one Lord Janārdana alone assumes the designations of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, who perform the acts of creation, preservation, and destruction.
Thus, because Rudra is the very body of the Lord, he possesses the status of the Supreme Maheśvara. Being such as this—
Having meditated upon Rudra, the sage—one whose nature is contemplation—goes to the source of all beings, the cause of all causes, the protector of the sacrificial seat, who exists beyond darkness.

By such passages as "He who has the splendor of the sun, beyond darkness," he goes to—that is, attains—the Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa, who dwells on the far shore of darkness and is beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*). This is the meaning.
Furthermore, in this regard: by the words "May the auspicious God unite us with pure mindfulness," [it is implied that] one should desire health from the Sun, prosperity from Agni,
knowledge from Śaṅkara, and liberation from Janārdana.

Thus, because he bestows knowledge, the worship of Śaṅkara is taught. Therefore, an equality between Brahmā, Rudra, and others, on the one hand, and the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, on the other, is not tenable. As stated in the *Mahābhārata*: "Those who regard the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) with a sense of commonality—those indeed should be known as heretics, excluded from all sacred rites."
[The undesirable consequence for those who treat Nārāyaṇa with contempt due to his equality with Rudra and others:
But he who regards the god Nārāyaṇa as being on a par with others, goes to a terrible hell for as long as the moon and sun endure. (MBh.)

“O evil-minded one, he who even once declares the Great Viṣṇu to be equal to another inferior deity is an outcaste; he is not merely an outcaste—he is one who has abandoned his own kin. [Mahābhārata] In the Vārāha Purāṇa: “Those lowest of men who consider me to be equal to other deities...”
“They quickly descend to the state of a *caṇḍāla* for nine or five births,” so it is said in the *Varāha Purāṇa*.
And in the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata*:
“But he who disregards the divine Nārāyaṇa with an attitude of equality...”
[102.8] By that single act of contempt, one does not escape hell.
[102.9] For he who, being insentient, considers another to be superior—
[102.10] he should be known as a heretic (pāṣaṇḍin), excluded from all ritual actions.
Thus [in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.2.11].
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: "Those who, deluded by ignorance, declare another deity to be supreme [over Nārāyaṇa], the Lord of the World—they are indeed remembered as heretics. [Kūrma Purāṇa 10.2.12]
“But that twice-born man who regards the god Nārāyaṇa as being equal to deities such as Brahmā and Rudra would be a heretic,” so says the *Kūrmapurāṇa*.
Bhāradvāja said:
“Brahmā, Rudra, and the others are impure individual souls (*jīva*), who are manifestations (*vibhūti*) of Viṣṇu;
indeed, those of false views worship them as the Supreme Being.
Thus, in the *Vārāha-purāṇa*, Rudra says to Agastya:
“The god who is worshipped with sacrifices, from whom this entire world has arisen,
and in whom all that is moving and unmoving is always dissolved—
he is the supreme god Nārāyaṇa, Janārdana, whose form is *sattva*. [VarāhaP 102.18–20]

[102.21] That Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, manifested himself in three ways. [102.22] The all-pervading Lord himself was born as the Pure Being (Śuddhasattva), consisting of the qualities of passion (rajas) and goodness (sattva). [102.23] He created Brahmā, whose seat is the lotus, within the lotus of his own navel.
“Endowed with *rajas* and *tamas*, that Lord also created me.
[VarāhaP] [103.1] Now, it is said: “It removes all sins here and subsequently destroys *saṃsāra*;
likewise, it may be fashioned from gold, silver, copper, and even iron. [VarāhaP]
“Likewise, having fashioned the *rayāṅga*, the eight-angled, the *sunābha*, and the *suvṛttaka* according to the prescribed rule, and having joined them with four flames,
one should heat them in the fire according to the ritual and wear them endowed with devotion. Thus [it is said in the Varāha Purāṇa].
“Sacrifice, charity, austerity, fire-offerings, feeding, and libations for the ancestors—
all these become fruitless for a Brahmin who lacks the mark of the discus. [Varāha Purāṇa] (103.6–8) At a funeral rite, a gift, a vow, a sacrifice, a marriage, or the initiation ceremony...”

“If one should worship only a Brahmin marked with the discus and no other”—by such statements as these, since one who is not marked with the discus and so forth lacks the status of a Vaiṣṇava, how can the Vaikhānasas be considered Vaiṣṇavas? To this it is replied:
[the Vaikhānasas possess the status of Vaiṣṇavas even though they are not marked with the discus and so forth].
“From the scriptural tradition: ‘He who, while still in the womb, holds a wheel in his hand to bestow upon me boundless glory—he becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin).
And: ‘Among all the Vaikhānasas, those born from the womb of Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa himself bears his own mudrā within the womb.’”

“Having said ‘Sudarśana’ while facing it, one should hold the Sudarśana discus in the right hand; and saying ‘Ravipāṃ,’ one should hold the conch in the left hand. [The Vaiṣṇava nature of the Vaikhānasas from the womb.]

And because it was stated thus by Bhṛgu, through the rite of offering oblations to Śrī Viṣṇu, the status of being born with Viṣṇu within the womb (*garbhavaiṣṇavatva*) and so forth is attained by the *Vaikhānasas*.
Likewise: "The objects are indeed superior to the senses, and the mind is superior to the objects;
the intellect is superior to the mind, and the Great Self (*mahān ātmā*) is superior to the intellect."
[103.21] "Greater than the Great is the Unmanifest; greater than the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa.
[103.22] There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the ultimate limit, that is the supreme goal.
[The attainment of refuge for one who has entered the womb.]

Thus, according to scripture, even for one in the womb, *prapatti* (surrender) is possible by means of bringing the Supreme Person under control through supreme single-minded devotion (*paramaikāntitva*).
Regarding this, the possibility of *prapatti* for one in the womb is heard in the *Garbhopaniṣad*: "Through knowledge and meditation, he contemplates the Imperishable, the syllable *Oṃ*.

Having said this, it continues: "Then, in the ninth month, he becomes endowed with all characteristics. He remembers his previous birth. His performed and unperformed actions become manifest, and he experiences the fruits of his good and evil deeds."
“Thousands of different wombs have indeed been seen by me;
various foods have been eaten, and various breasts have been drunk from.
Having been born and having died, birth occurs again and again.”
Alas! I am submerged in suffering; I see no remedy.
Having said this, [GarbhaU 4.2] [104.7]:
“If I am released from the womb, I shall take refuge in that Nārāyaṇa,
the one who brings about the destruction of the inauspicious and bestows the fruit of liberation,” [GarbhaU 4.6] [104.8].

In the *Puruṣasūktabhāṣya*—in the *Mudgalopaniṣad*: “Vāmadeva, though being the son of Aṅgiras, while still lying within the womb of his mother Anasūyā after having performed worship for many nights, came to know Brahman itself. Having burst open the front of the womb, he ascended to the world of Brahman. As he was departing, Indra spoke to him midway on the path; thus the Upaniṣads declare.”
"O Blessed One, while remaining attached right within the womb-cage, one who is unacquainted with the means— thinking 'I have departed from this by some small measure'—
reaches the further shore of the path," and so forth. Thus, it is indeed possible for one situated in the womb to engage in practices such as taking refuge and reflecting upon the Dharma.
[The twofold nature of *prapatti* according to the distinction between Vedic and Tantric:

[104.15–16] *Prapatti* is of two kinds, distinguished as Vedic and Tantric. That which is preceded by the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) and includes the invocation (*āvāhana*) of Puruṣa and others is the Vedic [form]. [The definition of Vedic *prapatti*]
In another Vedic scripture:
“By the syllable *a*, Viṣṇu is expressed—the Lord of all worlds, Hari;
likewise, by the syllable *u*, Lakṣmī is expressed as she was uplifted by Viṣṇu.”
“The letter *ma*, however, is the servant of those two; such is the definition of the *praṇava*.
Furthermore, it is heard in scripture that by the mere utterance of the *praṇava*, even the bearing of the conch, the discus, and so forth, becomes possible.
In the *Kaivalyopaniṣad*: “One who has applied the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) and bears the discus meditates upon Viṣṇu, the Supreme.”

“He who is the Great Soul, who by his voice and mantra is eternally situated in the heart— that which is higher than the high, greater than the great. Thus, the Vedic *prapatti* (surrender) consists solely in the constant contemplation that [the Lord] is the cause of all, the protector of all, the sovereign of all, the Lord of Śrī, and one’s own natural subordinate (*śeṣa*).
“If you have a desire for your own livelihood, if you have a longing for your own existence, then always remember that Hari is the master, you are His servant, and this is your very nature.
Thus it is established in the Sūtra.
In the *Pāñcarātra*, however, it says:
"Having abandoned the Triple Veda (*trayī*), they have taken refuge in the Tantra alone."
Thus, [PadmaSa Caryāpāda 21.56cd]:
“Prapatti, or taking refuge, is the petitioning for one’s own desired goal—which cannot be accomplished by any other means—with great confidence, making that alone the sole means. [105.6–105.7]

And thus it is taught. Because that [tantric] surrender (prapatti) is performed only once, lacks the accompaniment of mantras, and lacks the recollection of the path remaining after it, the author of the Sūtras—setting aside that tantric surrender—has prescribed only the Vedic surrender, in accordance with the Śruti text: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, that alone becomes more powerful."
[The branding with the heated discus and other marks is not for the twice-born.

In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "The branding with the conch, discus, mace, and so forth is prescribed for those initiated into the *tantras* of Viṣṇu’s tradition and others, but not for other embodied beings. [SkandaP 105.11–12]
[105.13] “The horizontal *tripuṇḍra* mark should be worn by those who have received initiation (*dīkṣā*) according to the *Śiva-āgama* and other such traditions.

[Skanda Purāṇa] [105.14] Viṣṇu says: “The marking of the body with the conch, the discus, and so forth, as well as singing, dancing, and the like—this is the duty of the once-born (*ekajātī*), and it should never belong to the twice-born (*dvijaman*). [Viṣṇu Purāṇa]
In the tenth book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam:
“To Trivakrā was born a son named Upaśloka, who was devoted to Kṛṣṇa;
he was a direct disciple of Nārada and possessed an undivided mind.”
Therefore, he spoke the Sāttvata Tantra, by knowing which one becomes a partaker of liberation;
in it, the Vaiṣṇava consecration is prescribed for women, Śūdras, and slaves.
Thus, in the *Padma Purāṇa*, [regarding the definition and other characteristics of Tantric surrender]: [105.21] *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*.
“O best of kings, it is heard in the Tittiri recension: ‘All the deities eternally abide in the Brāhmaṇa who knows the Vedas.
On the right shoulder of the Brāhmaṇa dwells the bearer of the conch, the discus, and the mace.”
[105.24] Hari stands on the left, out of respect for the son of Devakī.
[PadmaP] [106.1] Therefore, this body of the Brahmin is called a temple (devatāgāra).
[106.2] When it is burned, all the deities flee in the ten directions. [PadmaP]
[The one entitled to the rites of the heated wheel, mark, and so forth:
"That lowest of Brahmins who burns down a house becomes a burner of that [sacred fire];
he who makes a conch or a wheel out of clay or heated iron [is likewise]. (Padma Purāṇa)

“He is to be excluded from all the duties of the twice-born, like a Śūdra; just as wood grown in a cremation ground is unfit for all ritual acts, so too a Brahmin marked with the discus is censured in all ritual acts. [PadmaP]
In that very same work: "If a Brahmin, whether out of delusion or even greed, is marked with the wheel-sign, he is to be known as unworthy for the rites prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis.
He becomes unfit for ritual acts, just like wood that has gone to the cremation ground. [Padma Purāṇa]
“Likewise, those who have been branded with the wheel and other marks are unfit for all ritual acts.
That village or even that district where a person exists whose body is half-burned by such marks should be known as a cremation ground; it is unfit for the twice-born to dwell in. [Padma Purāṇa]

The refutation has been stated with these words beginning with [106.14–16]. It is understood that these statements prescribing the branding with the heated discus (*taptacakrāṅkana*) pertain specifically to those initiated according to the methods taught in the Tantric scriptures, because it is stated that they apply to "those initiated in the *Viṣṇvāgama* and other tantras," because they are stated to concern only a single caste (*ekajāti*), and because it is stated that they do not apply to "other embodied beings" (*nānyadehinām*).

Alternatively, in order to avoid the futility of injunctions and prohibitions, this has been set forth in the Śrī Vaikhānasa Śāstra as a form of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) accompanied by mantras, according to the logic of such Vedic passages as: "He touches with the two omentum-spits; that is neither touched nor untouched," and "That is indeed smelled, yet neither eaten nor uneaten. As follows:
“Having spoken of the Sudarśana, one should hold the Sudarśana on the right,
and on the left, one should bear the *ravipā* and the conch in the hand,” thus it is said in the *Mahopaniṣad*, in the *Brahmasūkta*.
“A Brahmin should indeed bear the *sudarśana* on his right arm, and he should bear the conch (*śaṅkha*) on his left; so say those who know the Vedas.
[Thus, there is a lack of universal eligibility for the bearing of the heated discus as taught in the *Pāñcarātra*.]

[The Pāñcarātra and other systems as delusive scriptures] [107.1] Some say that because it is a delusive scripture and because its subject matter is cursed, the practice of *tāpa* (scorching/initiation by fire) is prescribed in the *Pāñcarātra*.
[107.2] In the *Padmapurāṇa*, Gautama says:
“Since such deceit was practiced by those who merely resemble Brahmins toward me, who am upright,
they have consequently fallen from the path of the Vedas and become sinners.
[This applies to those in] the Kālamukha, Pāñcarātra, Kālapāla, and Śāmbhava [sects].”
[107.5] “And you who have been initiated into the Śākta [tradition] shall become the lowest of Brāhmaṇas.
[PadmaP] [107.6] Brahmā said: “O Hari, those twice-born who are initiated into the Buddhist, the Bhāgavata, and thirdly the Pāñcarātra tantras, shall always be free from fear. [PadmaP]
In the auspicious practice of the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, which grants immediate liberation,
those who are constantly averse to devotion to you shall remain utterly deluded.
[They shall be marked] by the conch, the *vīṇā*, the discus, the mace, the thunderbolt, the noose, the goad, and so forth.
[107.11] “Marked by faith, you shall become the lowest of Brahmins.
Thus [in the *Padma Purāṇa*]. [107.12] In the *Skānda Purāṇa*, in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*, Rudra says to Sarasvatī:
[107.13] “O fair-eyed one, it has been said that among the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), Śruti is the most powerful,” beginning thus [in the *Skanda Purāṇa*].
“O believer, the paths such as the *Pāñcarātra* have their root in the Veda;
for they do not exist independently, and thus, O embodied one, they are not based on error.
Nevertheless, that portion which is not contradicted by the Vedic path...”
[107.17] It is said that this portion is the authoritative means for certain qualified persons. [107.18–19] But for those living beings who have utterly strayed from the Vedic path,
the Pāñcarātra and other such paths are beneficial only through the power of time.
O Great Goddess, for the practitioners of Tantra, it cannot be attained without mediation.
Thus it has been established.
[SkandaP] [107.21] In the *Kūrma-purāṇa*: “In ancient times, in the holy Dāruvana forest, there were sages who were householders...
[KūrmaP 16.97ab] [107.22] Beginning with this, and having described everything from the fabrication of the cow through illusion up to the receipt of the curse:
“O Great God, what shall be our livelihood? You ought to save us from this curse.
Then, having gazed upon Viṣṇu standing by his side, the Bull-bannered One [spoke regarding how the Pāñcarātra was set forth for those who had fallen away from the Vedas].
"What would be the purpose of these seekers of merit? he asked.
Then the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the refuge of all and the one who is affectionate toward his devotees, Hari, looked upon the great lords of brahmins as they bowed down and spoke to Gopati.
O Śaṅkara, not even a trace of merit is found in a scripture outside the Vedas,
since Dharma has indeed issued forth from the Veda alone.
Nevertheless, O Maheśvara, out of affection for your devotees, it must be protected.

"O bull-bannered one, there is no doubt that all these brahmins have been deceived by us both. Therefore, for the sake of protecting those who are outside the Vedas and for the sake of deluding the wicked, we shall compose various scriptures."

Thus urged by Mādhava, the enemy of the Asuras, Rudra composed treatises of delusion; and Keśava, likewise impelled by Śiva, did the same. These include the Kāpāla, Yāmala, Vāma, Bhairava, Pūrva, and Paścima.
Having composed and worshipped the Pāñcarātra, the Pāśupata, and likewise thousands of other [systems], and performing therein what is enjoined there,
they fall again and again into terrible hells for many kalpas.

And so it has been said [in Kūrma Purāṇa 16.120]: “O child, one should not look at a man who has been excluded during the time of worship. And in the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā of the Skanda Purāṇa [108.17]: “One should not look at a man who has been cast out during the time of worship.”
“Those lowest of Brahmins who were cursed by Dadhīca and Gautama shall descend in the Kali age, being censured and excluded,” so it is said in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Furthermore, in the *Sāmba Purāṇa*:
"One who has fallen away from the revealed scripture (*śruti*) and feels fear regarding the expiations prescribed in the traditional law (*smṛti*),
should gradually take recourse to the *tantra* for the sake of accomplishing the *śruti*.
Indeed, that which ends only with death is proclaimed in the *Dharmaśāstra* and the *Purāṇa*."

[108.23] For humans who are most wicked, the expiation is extremely severe. [SāmbaP] [The exclusion from the Śrauta and Smārta paths for those following the Pāñcarātra system] [109.1] A great fear arises in those of weak minds at the time of death.
"For the sake of protecting them alone,
I have spoken that Tantra— the Pāñcarātra, the Bhāgavata Tantra known by the name Sāttvata—
which the Lord of Kamalā spoke, directed toward those who had fallen away from the Vedas. Thus [it is said in the Sāmba Purāṇa].
Elsewhere it says: "Now, there was a powerful and high-souled devotee of Viṣṇu named Aṃśu Sāttvata, who was devoted to charity and the best among those skilled in the science of archery."
Following the words of Nārada, he became devoted to the worship of Vāsudeva and promulgated a scripture that was frequented by the Kuṇḍas, Golakas, and others.
“Indeed, by his name, the magnificent and great scripture known as the *Sāttvata*—which brings benefit to Kuṇḍa and others—is promulgated.
Thus it is said in the *Vāsiṣṭha*: “O Bṛddhaśāvaka, those people who know the *Pāñcarātra* are free from worldly scent (passion).”
The Kāpālikas, the Pāśupatas, and those who are like them—
these wicked-minded ones of a tamasic nature— who eat his sacrificial offerings,
for him that scripture shall be of no avail, nor shall its fruit exist either in this world or after death.
Thus [in the Vasiṣṭha Dharmasūtra, 109.15].
In the Liṅga Purāṇa, in the ninth chapter on the characteristics of the Yugas (yugadharma), [109.16]: “And they will become marked with the insignia of the weapons of the deities.”
[109.17] They will not hear of Nārāyaṇa when the end of the age has arrived.

[LiṅgaP] [109.18–19] O best of sages, O Brahmin, in the Kali age, men will never perform other rites, whether they be those prescribed by the Vedas (śrauta) or those based on tradition (smārta). [LiṅgaP]

“O Sage, O Brahmin, in the Kali age they will say that the sacred tradition, the Dharmaśāstras, the Purāṇas, and the Mahābhārata are of little importance. O best of sages, they will not perform the rites prescribed by the Vedas with faith.”
[109.23] In the Kali age, the Brahmins have no taste for their own dharma.
[LiṅgaP] [109.24] O Sage, some praise the Pāñcarātra, while others praise the Bhāgavata; [109.25] some desire the Kāpāla, and others the Pāśupata, O Sage. [LiṅgaP]

[The necessity of performing the wheel-marking through the form of meditation] [110.1] Some praise the Buddhist [system], and likewise some the Digambara; [110.2] some, O Brahmin, the Lokāyata, and some the Soma, O Great Sage. [Liṅga Purāṇa]
Some desire the Lākula [tradition], while others likewise desire the Bhairava;
some praise the Vāma, and others likewise the Śākta;
some desire the Śāmbhava, and some on earth desire the Yāmala.
[110.6] O Great Sage, there are other treatises that are contradictory;
[110.7] some are sellers of holy places, while others are sellers of deities;
[110.8] some are sellers of milk, and others are sellers of clarified butter.
“In the Kali age, there will be men who sell meat, others who sell liquor, some who sell their sons, others who sell their wives,
and some who even sell their husbands. Thus it is said in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*.
[110.12] Therefore, it is established that the wearing of the heated discus (*taptacakradhāraṇa*) as taught in the *Pañcarātra* is not common to all.
[110.13–16] Now, as for what was said—that it is not common to all—that is untenable; for in the *Atharvaṇa*:
"He who bears upon his body the heated discus, the power of the immeasurable Viṣṇu, the god of gods—he goes to the firmament, beyond misfortunes..."

If it is argued that ascetics who are free from passion depart having shaken off [the body], because [this] is heard in the scriptures as being common to all, such as in the passage beginning, "The foot is pure, spread out, ancient" (*caraṇaṃ pavitraṃ vitataṃ purāṇam*), [we reply: no;

for there is a prescription of penance regarding the wearing of the heated discus. Therefore, [liberation occurs] only through the path already described, which consists of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

The marking with the disc is not performed by means of branding with fire. The scriptural passage common to all, however, refers to those other than the Vaikhānasas, because the determination of its meaning must be made in a way that does not contradict such scriptural passages as, "Of whom [I am] the glory," and so forth. Therefore, the branding of the disc with fire is not common to all.
Furthermore: "O Bhārata, in whatever matter the course of the scriptures differs regarding all ritual acts—
such as the distinction between the oblation offered after sunrise and that offered before sunrise—
that which is more authoritative, O mighty-armed one, prevails even over what is declared in all other scriptures."
[110.24] Thus, according to the recollection of Sumantu, a settled alternative must be stated here:
[Viṣṇu alone is the agent of destruction].

[111.1–2] Furthermore, it is heard in scripture that Hari alone is the agent of the destruction even of Brahmā, Rudra, and the others. In the Yajurveda: “The gods follow Hari as he withdraws [the world], the Lord of the universe, the bull among thoughts.”
Thus, here the Telugu is verified: [The reason for the worship of Rudra performed by Viṣṇu] [111.3] In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
“Because he seizes and brings under control Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Yama, and Varuṇa as well, he is therefore called Hari here.
Brahmā, Śambhu, likewise Arka, Candramas, and Śatakratu...”
“In this way, these and others likewise are joined with the splendor of Viṣṇu;
yet at the conclusion of their worldly duties, they are separated from that splendor, and all of them return to the five elements. Thus [it is said in the *Brahma Purāṇa*].

[111.9-14] If it is argued: "Is it not the case that in the Yajus-mantra previously cited, 'hariṃ harantam' (carrying Hari), the word *īśāna* is heard; therefore, it is revealed in scripture that Rudra alone is the agent of dissolution?"—that is incorrect. For in that context, by the words "lord of the universe" (*viśvasyeśāna*), his status as the controller of the world is expressed. And thus, just as in the passage "the lord of the universe, the master of himself," it is Nārāyaṇa alone who is the subject to be established here. [As it is said: "The mistress of this world is the wife of Viṣṇu"; he is Hari, the most excellent of the wise.
“May the waters swell for Indra,” “Thou art Virāj,” “The Bṛhatī, Śravasī, Indrapatnī, Dharmapatnī,” “He is Brahmā, he is Śiva, he is Indra.”
Such scriptural passages as these are to be considered here.
Now, in the eighth chapter of the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, in the summary of the *Rāmāyaṇa*:
"Having constructed a bridge across the great ocean with hundreds of monkeys at the gate of Laṅkā... [KūrmaP 21.44cd]
“The Lord, whose nature is the supreme Dharma, slew Rāvaṇa at the Setu.
Having thus explained the slaying of Rāvaṇa and other events, [the text continues]:
“In the middle of the Setu is Mahādeva, the Sovereign (Īśāna), clad in an elephant hide.”
Rāghava established the deity in the form of a *liṅga* and worshipped him;
thereupon the Lord Mahādeva, Śaṅkara, together with Pārvatī,
appeared visibly before him and granted him an excellent boon.

If it is argued that "the status of Rudra as a bestower of boons was obtained through the grace of Viṣṇu" (112.1–2), and thus the worship of the Lord by Rudra is being described—this is true. Even that [status] of Rudra was obtained through the grace of the boon granted by the Blessed One. For it is stated thus in the *Rudragītā* within the ancient history (*itihāsa*) of the *Vārāha-purāṇa*:
as follows—
Rudra said to Agastya:
“In the past, I was created by Brahmā and told, ‘Create offspring.
O twice-born one, being ignorant and incapable, I sank into the water.”
Beginning thus, [VarāhaP 112.6–7]:
In the midst of the waters, Rudra beheld a certain exceedingly beautiful person, lotus-eyed, resembling a dark cloud; when asked by Rudra, "Who are you?", his reply was:
[112.8] "I am the eternal god Nārāyaṇa, reclining upon the waters."
May you possess the divine eye; by means of it, behold me with diligence.
Having established this, [the Varāha Purāṇa states]:
“When he was thus addressed by him, as soon as I looked at his body, I saw it to be only the size of a thumb, yet possessing the blazing splendor of the sun.”
I beheld him alone; in his navel was a lotus.
There I saw Brahmā, and from his body, I saw myself.
Having thus seen that Great Soul, I then attained a state of joy.
“O tiger among the twice-born, the thought arose in me to praise him.
Having thus begun and recited a great hymn of praise, at the conclusion Rudra presented his desired request to the Blessed One, as follows:
“Thus have I praised you, O Blessed One; take pleasure in me, especially since I am your devotee.”
“Command me to create the creation; grant omniscience to me—homage be to you, O Viṣṇu!
[VarāhaP] When the hymn had thus been completed: “Choose a boon! May it be well with you, O God of gods, Lord of Umā! [VarāhaP]
Thus enjoined by the Blessed One, Rudra said: "O Lord, I have been told by Brahmā, 'Create living beings.
In that regard, O Creator of Beings, bestow upon me the threefold knowledge."
Thus he prayed. [VarāhaP] [Viṣṇu’s role as the destroyer of Rudra in the form of the Śarabha, etc.
[113.1] Then the Blessed Lord said:
“You are omniscient, there is no doubt; you are the eternal mass of knowledge.
You shall always be worthy of worship by the gods at all times.
When this had been said, the Lord of Umā joyfully spoke these words once more:
"O God, grant me another boon that is well-known among all living beings:
having become a mortal, may you yourself worship me, O Keśava!
And since you carry me, O Lord of Gods, accept a boon from me as well."
By which I became more worthy of worship than all the gods.
Thus requested again by him,
the Blessed Lord said:
"Having assumed human form for the sake of accomplishing the work of the gods..."
“I shall worship you alone; and may you be the granter of boons to me.
O God of gods, Lord of Umā, as for what was said by you—‘Carry me’—I shall carry you, O God, having become a cloud, for a hundred years.”
Thus he granted even a boon.
[113.13] “In this very same way, the divine Hari, the Lord of All, the Creator of All, became the granter of boons to me in the past; therefore I was chosen by the deities. [VarāhaP.]
“There has never been, nor will there ever be, a deity superior to Nārāyaṇa.
This is the secret of the gods and the ancient seers, O best of beings. Thus [it is said in the Varāha Purāṇa]. Furthermore:
In the *Śrī Viṣṇupurāṇa*: “Among gods, animals, and humans, this play consisting of the assumption of bodies is the manifestation of your activity as the Self of all beings. (*Viṣṇupurāṇa*)
“[The forms] called gods, animals, and humans, which possess movement by their own grace, exist for the benefit of the worlds; they are not born from the cause of karma.

[Viṣṇu Purāṇa] In this way, it is understood from the *Nārasiṃha Purāṇa* and other texts that even Brahmā, Rudra, and the others who approached Him in the form of a *śarabha* were annihilated by the Blessed One in His form as Nṛsiṃha. As it is said:
[The manner of the manifestation of Śarabha,
etc. [114.1] Immediately after the slaying of Hiraṇyaka, there, in the thirty-seventh chapter:
“Bṛhaspati said to the gods, including Indra, who were terrified by Hiraṇyakaśipu:
‘Go to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk and there praise Keśava.
When Viṣṇu is praised by you, he will become gracious in an instant.’”
Beginning with these words, [NarasiṃhaP 114.5–6]:
“O subduers of the asuras, I know all about your arrival;
I was praised by Śaṅkara for the sake of destroying Hiraṇyaka.”
Having said this, immediately after the slaying of Hiraṇyaka, [it is said]:
"Of that Nṛsiṃha, the Lord of the World, who was overcome by anger..."
[114.9] "Having seen that terrifying form, the gods and dānavas were struck with fear.
[NarasiṃhaP] [114.10] Having begun thus and spoken the hymn of praise, and having subsequently established the account of his approaching Brahmā and so forth:
[114.11] "When that Blessed One, Nṛsiṃha, the Supreme Self, was enraged..."
[114.12] This entire world trembles violently when the Lord of Gods is enraged.
[114.13] Indeed, there exists no other refuge for the gods here than you.
[114.14] O Hari, born as Narasiṃha, destroy this fear of mine!
Having stated the prayer to Rudra and so forth with these words, [the text continues]:
“Hiraṇyakaśipu, the Daitya of great strength, has been slain by him; who shall pacify the wrath of that Hari-medhas? [Narasiṃha Purāṇa]
"You are my progenitor, O Lord, but Hari is your progenitor.
Who indeed would be capable of restraining that god Viṣṇu?
Out of fear of him the wind blows, and out of fear of him the sun shines."
[114.21] Since the earth itself supports him out of fear, who would be the master to subdue him?
[114.22] Nevertheless, through supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*), a means is visible to me. [114.23] Once that is accomplished, there will be welfare; remaining silent does not please me.
The buffalo is the enemy of horses; the lord of beasts is the enemy of elephants. Likewise, the ram is known to be the enemy of monkeys, and the *garuḍa* is the enemy of serpents.

[The followers of Kātyāyana’s Sūtras lack exclusive devotion to the Supreme.

[116.23–117.2] Therefore, because Bodhāyana has established the equality of Nārāyaṇa with Rudra, and because the sixfold marks of purport (*ṣaḍvidhatātparyaliṅga*) are absent in the Sūtras of Bodhāyana, Āpastamba, and others, they lack exclusive devotion to Nārāyaṇa alone from the time of creation onwards, as their practice is seen to involve the worship of various deities.
Furthermore, absolute single-minded devotion is not possible. Likewise, for those who follow the *Kātyāyana-sūtra*:
"With mantras dedicated to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Savitṛ, Mitra, and Varuṇa—using only those mantras bearing their respective marks—one should worship with a concentrated mind."
Because it is established thus in the *Kātyāyanasūtra* [117.5], there is no absolute exclusivity.
However, in the *Drāhyāyaṇasūtra*, taking refuge (*prapadana*) at the commencement of a ritual act is taught as being directed toward Rudra [117.6].

Therefore, it is appropriate to state the formal proposition (*pratijñā*) that supreme single-minded devotion (*paramaikāntitva*) belongs exclusively to the venerable Vaikhānasas because of their exclusive dedication to the glorious Nārāyaṇa alone. Thus, the ninth reason—“because of exclusive dedication to the glorious Nārāyaṇa, the sole cause of the entire universe”—has been defined.
This concludes the definition of the ninth reason.

The Śruti also says: “May I attain that beloved goal of his, where men devoted to the gods rejoice; for there, in the highest step of Viṣṇu of the wide stride, is the spring of honey—such indeed is his kinship. The meaning of this is as follows:

Proceeding thus every day, he is a "kinsman of Viṣṇu, the wide-striding one"— the singular number is used for the genus. He alone is exceedingly beloved in the "supreme" (*parame*), that is,
in the most excellent "honey" (*madhve*).
Eager for the "fountain" (*utsa*) in the most enjoyable state of Viṣṇu’s abode, which is like honey; or rather, "excellent" (*utkṛṣṭa*).

[ĀS] [122.4–7] According to the manner thus established, since there is an absence of accessibility in the Blessed One’s supreme nature and so forth, for the sake of reviving the entire world...

The arcāvatāra (the descent as an image). Because they are solely devoted to that [arcāvatāra], the Vaikhānasas are the most beloved of the Lord. Since Bodhāyana, Āpastamba, and others lack this exclusive devotion solely to Nārāyaṇa, it is in no way possible for them to possess the status of *paramaikāntins* (supreme monotheists) or to be the most beloved of the Blessed One.

Thus, it is established that only the Vaikhānasas can appropriately possess supreme monotheism and the state of being the most beloved of the Blessed One; therefore, everything is consistent. This concludes the exposition of the tenth reason.
